title: Rarefaction, condensation, alteration and the discontinuity objection (I.261–263)
en:
### Rarefaction, condensation, alteration and the discontinuity objection (I.261–263)

Some argue for actual rarefaction and condensation from observable changes of volume—freezing and melting—or the air in a bottle under suction and compression. In a bottle partly evacuated, if the air left did not expand, **a void** would arise; on blowing into it, if the air did not compress, **interpenetration of bodies** would occur. These arguments rely on their own physical assumptions. “Rarefaction” is also used in a second sense for **dispersion**, the moving apart of a body's constituents so that another material, such as air, enters the interstices; condensation is **aggregation** or packing closer so that foreign material leaves. These are changes in **relative arrangement** rather than the same subject's receiving a distinct continuous magnitude. They can be analyzed as local movements of parts, quantitative change of the whole, and positional change in their mutual arrangement.

The fourfold division of quantitative changes is not exhaustive. **Swelling** increases magnitude through added material but not by the natural proportions of growth. **Fattening** adds assimilated nourishment but not with proportional extension in **all directions**, and without a fixed developmental period or natural terminal proportion; **emaciation** is its reverse. Proper growth requires nutriment to penetrate openings in existing tissues, assimilate to their nature and move the original parts outward **proportionally** in all axes; true wasting reverses that process. In fattening new matter accumulates while the original organs do not themselves expand in the same growth-pattern. The word *dhubūl* is sometimes also used broadly for emaciation.

**“Fourth: quality.”** Gradual qualitative transformation is called **alteration** (*istiḥāla*): a grape turning from white to black or water from cool to hot. Some deny real alteration: heat is thought to result from **latent fiery particles** emerging, other fiery particles entering from outside, or certain parts of the water being **substantially transformed into fire**. Al-Taftāzānī rejects these substitutes. A very large mass of sulphur can ignite from a small flame; if the heat were only pre-existing or newly imported fire-particles, their quantity and sensory effects would require implausible assumptions. If parts of water became fire, they ought to rise through their natural tendency or be quenched by the cold wet remainder; the philosophical theory of elemental transformation also requires intermediate conversion through **air**. Transformation of quality therefore cannot simply be dismissed as mechanical particle displacement or sudden generation and corruption.

**“The truth.”** The author now introduces a more radical qualification: even **positional motion**, earlier accepted, has been traced back to local motion of parts; on strict analysis, **change in quantity and quality** also may not be true motion at all. Although we experience a body apparently moving gradually through increasing magnitudes or changing temperatures, distinct determinate magnitudes and qualities may in fact succeed one another **at discrete thresholds**, so close that we do not perceive the individual replacements. This resembles **earth transforming to water, then air, then fire**: the occurrence of multiple substantial transformations is not a single continuous substantial motion merely because its transitions form a sequence.

The argument is that if the intermediate **determinate states** between two magnitudes or qualities form a **finite** number, change must consist of successive indivisible steps, contradicting continuity and causing the familiar problem of indivisible spatial atoms and slower motion arising only from intervening pauses. If they form an **actual infinity** of distinct intermediates bounded by two extremes, an infinite plurality is allegedly contained between limits. The challenge, as stated, turns on treating each determinate intermediate as an **actually distinct, present item**, rather than allowing one continuum divisible only in thought. The author is deliberately distinguishing the **appearance of gradual change** from the stricter metaphysical notion of a truly continuous motion.

title: Motion outside four categories; natural, forced and voluntary movement (I.263–267)
en:
### Motion outside four categories; natural, forced and voluntary movement (I.263–267)

If motion is genuine continuous change, its continuous extended aspect must correspond to an underlying **continuum divisible without limit**, such as spatial distance, rather than to a **finite collection of actually distinct intermediate forms**, however internally divisible one later calls each intermediate. This supports the analysis of local movement but counts against taking a succession of determinate qualities or magnitudes as one motion. The objection that magnitude itself is indefinitely divisible misses the claim: the change **from one determinate magnitude to another** may still be by discrete replacement, not a continuous change of a single magnitude.

**“Motion is not established in the remaining categories.”** The remaining candidates are substance, when, relation, possession, acting and being-acted-upon. In **substance**, the successive reception of forms by matter is commonly held to involve **generation and corruption**, not gradual intensification of one substantial form. Some argue a substance cannot admit degrees: either the former species remains, in which case modification belongs to its accidents, or it perishes, in which case the replacement is not intensification. Another argument claims that substantial form constitutes the actuality of matter, so if that form perishes, the material subject itself perishes and no one enduring subject of motion remains. The reply invokes matter's continuity through **different forms of the same generic kind**: it is constituted by having some form, not necessarily one individual form. Avicenna himself allows matter's individual identity to be retained through continuity at the specific level of form. The matter is not simply annihilated each time a form changes. A more sophisticated view denies substantial alteration because the persisting subject is essential to the concept of gradual increase, while successive substantial forms themselves cannot persist; this too requires further argument.

In **when (*matā*)**, shifting from one day to another is simply changing temporal attribution, not passing gradually through a new temporal quality. If when were itself the subject of a separate motion, a new when would be required for that motion, and so on. More substantively, time and temporal attribution are **dependent** on changes in other categories, just as relation depends on its foundation. In **relation** and **possession**, the supposed changes likewise follow changes in underlying things rather than stand alone. This is not merely because they are relational; *place* and *position* too involve relations but are treated differently. The point is their **lack of independent actuality** in relation to changing foundations.

A distinct motion in **acting** or **being acted upon** is contested. Suppose a thing switches from cooling to heating: if cooling continues, contrary effects overlap; if it stops before heating begins, there is no one continuous passage between them. Gradual waning of agency may instead belong to gradual fatigue of an instrument, weakening of intention or a change in the **receiving subject**, from which changes in the relational categories follow. Saying all relations by nature lack independent change would be too general, as one still needs to explain differences between the categories.

**“The moving subject”** requires no separate elaboration here. **“The mover.”** In the classical scheme motion may be (a) **accidental**, as a person carried along in a moving ship; (b) **violent/forced**, its mover external to the moved body; (c) **voluntary**, arising from an intrinsic or attached principle capable of awareness and intention, including a soul's relation to its body; or (d) **natural**, proceeding from intrinsic noncognitive nature. Voluntary and natural movers count as *in* the moving being whether they are bodily constituents or a soul specially joined to the body. Thus falling stones, human locomotion and rotation of celestial spheres were variously classified. On a thoroughgoing divine-creation theory these labels need not disappear: “mover” means the proximate **customarily concomitant created condition**, not an independent creator beside God.

**Breathing** can be called natural in its general necessity and voluntary in the power to advance, postpone or alter an individual breath. Sleeping people can execute actions classed as voluntary without present reflective awareness. **Organic growth** is straightforwardly natural on this account. **Heartbeat and arterial pulse**, though alternatively described as local, positional or quantitative movement, are also natural rather than effects of conscious volition or external violence. A single living nature can yield alternating **expansion and contraction**, since their aims are not to arrive at final opposite spatial boundaries but to draw in cooler air and expel corrupted air as the body requires. The claim that nature permits motion in only one direction applies primarily to **simple elemental bodies**, not plants and animals.

Another proposed taxonomy subdivides intrinsic motion into **simple and compound**, and distinguishes will-governed and non-will-governed compound movements, including plant growth and physiological pulse. The issue is not merely nomenclature but which proximal principle explains the act. Elemental natural motion requires the object's **particular nature together with absence from its natural situation**: neither the common nature of corporeality alone nor the particular nature by itself suffices, else bodies would be perpetually and uniformly moving. A displaced element moves **towards a condition fitting its nature**, not merely away from an unfitting one, and comes to rest when it arrives. Water may therefore move upward or downward depending on which natural ordering has been disturbed. “Seeking” a natural place here means directed tendency, not conscious intention.

title: Identity and diversity of movements (I.267–269)
en:
### Identity and diversity of movements (I.267–269)

**“Fourth investigation.”** Movements differ **essentially** or through accidents; they may be one **individually**, in **species**, or in **genus**, and admit discussion of contrariety and division. Six features have been distinguished, but three have a quasi-essential bearing on a movement's kind: **the category in which**, **the origin from which**, and **the terminus toward which** change occurs. The others—the moving subject, mover and time—are generally accidental to the definition of its species. Thus movements from equivalent beginnings to equivalent termini through one kind of change belong to **one species**, even if one is produced naturally by fire, another violently by a thrown stone and another voluntarily by a bird. The specific identities of subject and producer do not fix a movement's species, just as one sort of heat can inhere in a human or horse and originate from fire or sun. Different times also need not alter kind.

Movement from white to black **through yellow and red** differs from movement from black to white along the reverse order, even though they involve similar qualities, since their beginning and end differ. Movement from the same white to the same black through **yellow-red** differs from that through **green-blue**, because the **path within the category** differs. Similarly a journey between two fixed points along a straight line and one along a curve may be distinct in kind. A terse argument in the *Mawāqif* stating that the category must be one, else heating and blackening would differ, gives an **example**, not a full deduction; perhaps an original wording of “heating and cooling” was subsequently corrupted.

**Individual unity** of movement requires the same individual subject, time, and kind of category-path; a journey today is not the numerically same journey yesterday, nor movement of Zayd movement of ʿAmr. The identical path, in a strict individual sense, also fixes its **individual beginning and end**; consequently these need not be listed separately in the test of individual unity. It is not enough simply to require the same subject and time, since growth, warming, blackening or positional change can occur together. **Individual unity of mover** is not required: successive independent causes can act on different portions of one continuous process, just as successive heaters can maintain a single progressive warming or multiple pullers keep a body moving continuously. This does not mean two complete efficient causes independently produce precisely the same undivided effect: each acts on another **temporally distinguishable portion**, although the perceived continuum is one.

The object's being divisible **by thought** need not destroy continuity. There is, however, a conceptual difficulty: movement in the extended, imagined sense lacks **all its parts simultaneously** in the external world, whereas movement as **the intermediate condition** seems to have different actual states at different points. Al-Rāzī proposes that a single moving subject, time and continuous spatial interval suffice to give individual unity to the middle-state movement; the apparent plurality arises only from hypothetical boundaries of the path, which are not actual constituents. He regards this as a difficult matter. A criticism observes tension between describing motion's present middle-state as a single enduring actuality and admitting that its determinate state varies continuously, although it is not thereby a discrete collection of individuals.

title: Genus and species of motion; the grounds of contrary movements (I.269–272)
en:
### Genus and species of motion; the grounds of contrary movements (I.269–272)

Unity of **kind** depends on differences among the **category, origin and terminus**, whereas individual unity depends on individually fixed motion and subject. But the allegedly specific distinctions between **upper and lower regions** are less evident than those among qualities or magnitudes. Why treat the spatial state of a stone in lower air as differing in **species** from its state in upper air, when the only apparent difference is **distance from the earth's center or celestial boundary**, which is an accident of place? Similarly a straight versus curved course may differ through geometry, but a mile to the right and a mile to the left need not differ in category-species. At best the distinction of **straight and curved** magnitudes, treated by the philosophers as geometrically distinct kinds, is extended to movements traced upon them. In **ascent and descent**, al-Rāzī appeals to the opposition of **origin** and **end**, with direction up or down remaining naturally fixed under the ancient cosmology, unlike conventional left and right.

**“Generic unity.”** A common explanation says movements are of one genus if their **categories of change** are of one genus. Thus growth, wasting, rarefaction and condensation would fall under quantitative movement; changes among visible qualities within qualitative movement; and local versus positional movement in distinct genera. But this argument seems to assume that **motion itself has no universal genus**. If *motion* is univocal, it could be a genus common across these four kinds and the supposed dependence of genus upon the kind of subject would not be exclusive. The term manifestly has a common meaning—**gradual transition or first actuality of the potential**—not merely four unrelated homonyms. Some thinkers call it a **graded universal** (*mushakkik*) because it is an actuality and existence is graded. Yet the argument confuses **the concept of existence**, which may be graded, with all things **to which existence applies**; one cannot infer that the category of movement itself is graded merely because its instances exist by different degrees. Nor is it obvious that one movement is more intrinsically **movement** than another, as distinct from being faster, stronger or earlier in existence. One may suppose that motion is a separate highest genus above several Aristotelian categories, but that threatens the theory of ten ultimate categories. Others regard it as belonging to **being-affected**, even though changes occur across different substantive categories. A careful statement that movements of one subordinate genus share the genus of **the respect of change** avoids asserting the absence of every common essence of motion.

**“Contrariety of movements.”** Contrary motions do not become contrary merely because **the moving subjects** are contrary: hot and cold bodies can move in the same way, and one body can move in opposite ways. Nor because the **movers** are contrary: different movers can produce the same movement, and one voluntary mover can produce contrary movements. Nor through opposite **times**, which are not themselves opposite species. Nor simply through the category of change: **upward and downward** movements occur in the same spatial respect, as do whitening and blackening in the common colour category. The decisive factor seems to be **contrariety of starting and ending limits**, whether those limits are intrinsically contrary (white/black, maximum expansion/maximum wasting, erect/inverted posture) or opposed through their accidental natural situation (upper/lower extremities).

But the strict definition of contraries requires **two positive states**, excluding one another in the same subject at one time and under one respect, and being maximally distinct species of one genus. Ordinary upward and downward motions satisfy incompatibility, yet whether they are **maximally** contrary is contentious. One can draw a curve farther from a straight line than another; there are indefinitely many curved paths between two points, so a curved path chosen arbitrarily is not *the* maximal opposite of the straight. The same problem arises when an upward movement begins short of the natural lowest bound or ends short of the uppermost bound. Philosophers nonetheless call a stone's coerced upward motion contrary to its natural downward movement. A proposed resolution locates opposition in the **natural directions themselves**, which are contrary independently of the exact start and destination within them. This separates direction's essential natural determination from contingent points along the path, though its force depends upon the inherited cosmological framework.

title: Further objections to contrary motion; divisibility and speed (I.272–274)
en:
### Further objections to contrary motion; divisibility and speed (I.272–274)

Al-Rāzī stresses that a movement's first and last terms are opposed as **beginning and end**, because motion is related to them precisely **under those terms**, not merely as concrete point-individuals. Thus moving from A to B and from B to A reverses both its source and goal. An objection says the argument would classify **every reverse straight journey** as contrary, and even return movements on parts of circular routes. A possible answer is that full contrariety requires **maximal difference of determinate kind**, not merely relational inversion. A path from the zodiacal beginning of Aries to Libra and back along the chosen circular arc is arguably **local movement on a circle**, as with an ant walking round a turning mill, not purely **the positional rotation of the mill itself**. Since local and positional movements have different criteria, a general denial of contrariety of circular positional motions cannot automatically decide this case.

**“Divisibility.”** Motion and the **time and continuous magnitude** with which it corresponds admit mutually corresponding divisions: divide the journey's spatial course or its duration and the movement considered as an extended process is divided. Its starting and ending limits play a role but do not themselves constitute a collection of temporal parts. Division of the **mover** poses questions: a mover may be divisible or not, and parts of a divisible mover may or may not individually be able to produce movement. Division of the **moving body** also seems to divide the motion if it inheres throughout the subject like a colour in an extended thing. Yet whether an actual movement inheres in a body by **diffused inherence** requires demonstration; internal moving parts do not depart from one another, and separating a moving body into parts changes how we describe its motion without necessarily **cutting the originally continuous process into temporal pieces**. The proper quantitative division of an extended movement into halves, thirds and quarters occurs fundamentally by dividing **its interval or its time**, not merely by physically fragmenting the moving body.

**“Fifth investigation: speed and slowness.”** Every motion is in time and along a quantity-like extent, usually called **distance** even for changes in quality or magnitude. A subject can traverse the **same length in shorter time** or **a longer length in the same time** without changing the essence of local movement. Thus speed and slowness are treated as intensities or relational modes of a motion, recognized by their consequences: **faster** if it traverses equal length in less time or more length in equal time; **slower** under the reverse conditions. They vary **by comparison**: one motion may be faster than a second yet slower than a third. title: Can slowness consist of pauses? (I.274–276)
en:
### Can slowness consist of pauses? (I.274–276)

Three philosophical objections challenge the explanation of slowness through interspersed rests. (1) If two objects move **in the same time but across different distances**, the shorter journey must contain more rests according to the theory. Then there would be instants when the faster journey proceeds and the slower does not; but **conjoined movements** can remain inseparable despite their unequal distances, as the concentric circles of a rotating mill or arms of a compass. The shadow apparently moving in company with the sun is another image, though strictly a shadow may be a changing region of **illumination** rather than an accident undergoing local motion. The theologian can deny rationally necessary mutual accompaniment: even attached parts of a mill might, by divine power, fail to move synchronously. But such a reply allows physically coherent attachments to be disconnected without showing that the theory explains ordinary experience.

(2) During a slow motion, the complete causes and their proper conditions are present while obstacles are absent. A **pause** inserted during that period would make the sufficient cause fail to produce its effect. The voluntarist theologian replies that **God creates each event by choice**, including locomotion at one time and rest at another; a fixed created disposition is not an autonomous sufficient necessitating cause. On this strong view even “natural motion” becomes externally produced in the ultimate metaphysical sense.

(3) If ordinary earthly movement is extremely slow compared with the daily motion ascribed to the outermost celestial sphere, the pauses in a running horse, flying bird or arrow ought to vastly outnumber the instants of actual movement. We would then see it **resting vastly longer than moving**, contrary to sensory experience. The reply says the alternation is too fine for the senses to distinguish; the eye experiences the aggregate as one continuous motion. Al-Taftāzānī acknowledges the impressive force of the objections and comparative weakness of those replies.

**“Every speed and slowness admits degrees.”** Do they have absolute extrema—one movement so fast that it is not slow in any respect, or one so slow that it is not fast—or do they remain indefinitely comparable? The more plausible consequence of indefinitely divisible time and path is that **every actual motion can be slower than some possible one and faster than another**, because a similar path could hypothetically be traversed in half the time, or half the path in equal time. Al-Rāzī argues for limits on the basis that speed and slowness must exhibit **maximal opposition** for degrees to be intelligible. But the inference is weak: opposition and variation do not require physically realized absolute extremes. Even if finite natural regions and minimal traversable durations impose constraints, a purported slowest movement could still be compared to one taking longer on that same path, and a fastest to one travelling further in the same time. The daily rotation of the outermost sphere is **fastest among the celestial motions posited by that physics**, not necessarily among all **logically possible** motions.

title: Must a stationary interval separate contrary or angled movements? (I.276–278)
en:
### Must a stationary interval separate contrary or angled movements? (I.276–278)

**“Sixth investigation.”** Some philosophers and mutakallimūn claim that every two successive **straight-line movements** are separated by an interval of rest, whether the second retraces the first or turns at an angle. A **vertex-angle** exists in the latter case, not in simple reversal along one line; abbreviated formulations in the *Tajrīd* must not conflate those cases.

The principal philosophical argument treats **arrival at the limit** as occurring in an **instant** (*ān*), since otherwise arriving in one half of the alleged interval would disprove the attribution of the whole interval to arrival. The commencement of **departure** is likewise instantaneous. If these are **different instants** and instants cannot be immediately successive—else an extended continuum would consist of indivisible points—there must be **time between** them; with no motion in that interval, the subject rests. The weakness is the premise that arrival and initial departure cannot occur at **one shared boundary instant**, analogous to one geometrical point ending one segment and beginning another. Calling the first “arrival” and the second “not-arrival” does not imply the moving subject is both **at and not at** a place under one respect; it means one event terminates and another begins there.

A revised proof appeals to **two opposed inclinations**: an upward impulse causing arrival cannot coexist in the same instant with a downward impulse causing departure, so the old inclination ceases, the new begins, and a rest intervenes. But this assumes inclinations are **necessitating sufficient causes** and that the mathematical instant is an actually inhering temporal part, whereas in the continuum an instant is a **limit**, like a point on a line, and can be a common boundary. If the defender says a time interval is divisible only conceptually, why could two contrary impulses not succeed at one limit under distinct temporal respects? The objection does not imply that every present instant is an indivisible atomic duration.

It is then asked why the same argument does not force pauses whenever a moving body passes each **imaginary point** along a continuous straight line or a sphere touches successive points of a plane. The philosopher replies that these imagined boundaries have no independent existence as **actual endpoints**; the end of a genuinely interrupted motion, however, would constitute a real limit. Whether that distinction establishes a **nonzero** interval of rest remains disputed.

Al-Jubbāʾī argues for a pause specifically between a projectile's **upward and downward** movements. The coercive upward inclination gradually weakens until its strength equals the body's natural downward tendency; only after the natural inclination prevails does descent begin. At the instant of equality the body should be **stationary**. The answer distinguishes **rest at a nonextended transition instant** from an actual **duration of rest** between ascent and descent. The debate concerns the latter; no one denies that one movement ceases and the other begins.

Those denying a required pause add: if a stone remained still at the top after the upward impulse had ceased, nothing would continue weakening it through air resistance so descent could be postponed indefinitely; a pause would need its own physical cause, or else be infinitely divisible into a shorter pause with no necessary minimal length; and the argument would implausibly require a falling mountain to halt when it met a rising seed. Defenders reply that its internal natural tendency increases as the coercive one fades, that their equality can sustain temporary equilibrium, and that a microinterval may be indivisible **in the relevant physical respect** despite conceptual divisibility. Al-Taftāzānī notes these proposals and their counter-objections without granting a decisive empirical proof of a physically necessary pause.

title: Composite movements and rest in four categories (I.278–279)
en:
### Composite movements and rest in four categories (I.278–279)

**“Seventh investigation.”** A body can undergo **two motions at once**. A person walking toward the prow of a ship moving in the same direction recedes from the shore by the **sum** of the two displacements. Walking directly opposite the ship may yield no net displacement if speeds match, slow forward displacement if the ship prevails, or apparent backward motion if the person's pace prevails. This helps explain the observed **direct, stationary and retrograde appearances of planets** in composite celestial motion. If the two directions differ without being opposite, as a person moving north on a ship sailing east, the resulting displacement combines the components. More layers can be added, such as a person going east aboard a vessel propelled north by a river flowing west with a southerly wind: the body's resultant lies according to the combined motions. The argument is geometric and does not imply each component is a separate completed local change occupying the same isolated point.

**“Eighth investigation: rest.”** Rest (*sukūn*) is opposed to motion in the four categories where the latter is posited. In **place**, it is preserving the body's relation to relevant positional surroundings, remaining in one location. In **magnitude, quality and position**, it is preserving an actually attained kind without quantitative growth or wasting, qualitative intensification or weakening, or positional change. In that sense rest has a **positive determination** contrary to movement. Alternatively, rest means **privation of motion from a subject apt for it**, and then motion and rest oppose as **possession versus privation**. The qualification “apt for it” excludes absence of locomotion in an accident, an immaterial substance, an instantaneous beginning or ending of motion, or an allegedly fixed celestial sphere unable to leave its natural region. Al-Rāzī adds the stationary body in flowing water, whose surrounding envelope changes at every instant: it supposedly neither moves, since its position relative to external objects remains, nor rests, since it does not continuously stay in one enclosure. Al-Taftāzānī regards this as questionable.

The question which **rest** is opposed to which **movement** also demands qualification. Does movement along a path oppose rest at its beginning, at its end, or both? Does resting at one place oppose movement **away from** or **toward** that place? Properly considered, both relevant oppositions can obtain. If one means the rest **preceding** movement, it is at the origin and movement is away; if the rest **following** movement, it is at the destination and movement is toward it. It is wrong to argue that because rest at the destination is a **perfection of the moving body** it cannot be opposed to the movement: it is not a perfection **of movement as such**. A movement can terminate in its own nonexistence, undoubtedly opposed to it. Avicenna's attempt to restrict opposition to motion away from the **very place in which the body rests**, rather than motion to it, depends on reading rest as lack of motion **at that particular place**; the wider reading “not moving anywhere” is opposed to either kind of motion.

Rest is called **natural**, as a stone on the ground; **forced**, as a stone held suspended; or **voluntary**, as a bird hovering. Natural rest need not be caused by a special disturbance as natural motion is; nature simply retains its proper region when unconstrained. Rest is not itself composed of several rests, whereas motions can be described as composites of independently directed components. The claim that a human standing still has both natural and voluntary rest mistakes **different explanations or enabling conditions** for two distinct rests: the natural configuration maintains its position, while will may refrain from initiating movement. When more than one factor strengthens a movement, on the other hand, its **intensity** can genuinely increase rather than producing an additional separately counted act of locomotion.

title: Relations as reciprocal references: their forms, subjects and foundations (I.280–281)
en:
### Relations as reciprocal references: their forms, subjects and foundations (I.280–281)

**“Fifth chapter.”** **Relation** (*iḍāfa*) as an accidental genus is **recurring reference** (*nisba mutakarrira*): a reference intelligible only by comparison with a second reference which, in turn, is intelligible in comparison with the first. This is **relation in the strict sense** (*muḍāf ḥaqīqī*). The composite of relation and its bearer is the **relative in ordinary usage** (*muḍāf mashhūrī*). The bare underlying bearer by itself is not ordinarily called a “relative,” although ordinary grammar may say it “has a relation.” The philosophers first discuss the composite because concrete relative things are more readily apprehended than their abstract formal aspect.

A generalized definition calls a relative “that whose quiddity is conceived **by reference to another**.” The “other” must itself be conceived **by reference back to the first**; otherwise every concept with an evident, necessarily following implication would count as relational. The two concepts are **coordinate in intelligibility**, neither requiring a completed prior cognition of the other, as **father** and **son**. This is why relation requires **convertibility** (*inʿikās*): if the father is father **of the son**, the son is son **of the father**. Without attending to the precise respect the conversion fails: from “father of a human being” one cannot infer “the human being is a father.” To discover the relevant formal term, abstract away the features of one terminus until only the correlate remains; paternal reference persists while **sonship** remains and vanishes when sonship is removed, regardless of other attributes.

Reciprocal designation may or may not require prepositions or genitive relations; the verbal expressions can be symmetrical, as **greater/smaller**, or asymmetrical, like **master/slave**, **knower/known**, and **wing/bird possessing the wing**. The two references may have **the same formal name** on both sides, as fraternity, or **different forms**, as paternity and filiation. Some are **quantitatively determined**, as double and half, others merely comparative, as more and less. A relational qualification may presuppose **real qualities in both bearers**, as in lover and beloved according to one account (apprehension in the lover, beauty in the beloved); in only one, as knowing requires knowledge in the knower without requiring a symmetrical quality in the object; or in neither, as left and right may change purely by comparison of positions without intrinsic alteration.

Avicenna tentatively groups relational terms by **equality and comparison**, **excess** in magnitude or force, **action and passion** grounded in powers, and **representation or likeness**. His examples include stronger/weaker, agent/patient, father/son, and knowledge/known in which cognition resembles the known's form. He explicitly qualifies that the enumeration is not a complete rigorously delimited classification. A condensed quotation in the *Mawāqif* changes the arrangement and introduces union, likeness or adjacency in its own scheme; these two presentations must not be silently conflated.

Every existent may bear relations: the Necessary as first, a substance as father, a quantity as lesser, a quality as different, a place as higher, a temporal subject as earlier, a relation as nearer, a position as more upright, possession as more completely clothed, an action as more intense cutting, or a passion as more intense heating. Yet relation does **not** subsist as an independently existing thing alongside its bearer. Its determination is **its specified occurring or supervening upon something**. Thus *likeness* is a correspondence in a quality, formally a relation; the composite “a similarly coloured quality” is **a thing having a relation**, not the abstract category relation itself. Otherwise every derivative compound of an accidental category would have to be counted as an additional ultimate genus.

title: Correlates and the disputed external reality of relation; temporal attribution (I.281–283)
en:
### Correlates and the disputed external reality of relation; temporal attribution (I.281–283)

**“The correlates are coordinate.”** If a relation is taken **generally** on one side, its correlate is general; if one side is specified, the other is specified—for example double of **some number** corresponding to half in general, or the number **four** as double of **two**. Similar coordination applies, in the appropriate respect, to actual and potential, existing and nonexistent, intellectual and external reference. **Earlier** and **later** temporal events need not coexist: the mutually referred terms are the **concepts of priority and posteriority**, simultaneously conceived by the mind; the concrete events themselves occur successively. Indeed the two underlying bearers can exist independently, as father and son before a later child is born or one dies, or one may depend asymmetrically on the other, as knowledge on the knower, or they may be mutually co-dependent, as an essential cause and its proper effect. Reciprocal **intelligibility of reference** is not the same as reciprocal **existential dependence of bearers**.

**“This [does not settle external existence].”** Many mutakallimūn and some philosophers deny that **relation itself** is an independent external existent, giving three familiar arguments. (1) If a relation genuinely **inheres in a subject**, its inherence is another **relation**; that relation inheres through another, producing an infinite regress. (2) If relation **exists**, its being qualified by existence is another relation, supposedly requiring relation itself to exist beforehand: circularity. (3) Every number would have **infinitely many relational accidents**: two is half of four, a third of six, a fourth of eight, without end. The replies note that these objections, even if persuasive, exclude at most the claim that **every relation is a distinct external entity**, not the weaker possibility that **some** relations have external existence. A generic concept of relation might contain different species with different modes of reality. Conversely, appealing to apparently independent facts—“the sky is above us” or “Zayd is a father”—proves the **truth of the predication**, not yet that **above-ness or fatherhood is an extra inhering entity**. The statement “Zayd is blind” may be true without blindness being an additional positive entity.

Whether relations are **contraries** is also disputed. title: Position, possession, acting and being-acted-upon (I.283–285): completion of Accidents
en:
### Position, possession, acting and being-acted-upon (I.283–285): completion of Accidents

**“Among them is position (*waḍʿ*).”** Position is a disposition of a body arising from the **relations of its parts to one another** together with their relations to **relevant directions and to objects external to, or sometimes enclosed within, the body**. Standing upright involves the parts' specific arrangement—head upward, feet downward—while inversion is a distinct position although the same parts remain. A wholly enclosing body has positions assessed mainly by reference to what it encloses, while a wholly enclosed thing is also assessed by what surrounds it; intermediate cases admit both considerations. A position can be naturally fitting, as human uprightness, or contrary to nature, as inversion, and may be actual or potential. It admits strict contrariety, for upright and upside-down are incompatible positive dispositions maximally opposed in the relevant respect; it can also admit **degrees**, as in greater or lesser uprightness, bending and bowing.

**“Among them is having (*lahu*), called possession (*milk*) or equipment (*jiddah*).”** The category is sometimes defined as the **relation of a body to something surrounding it or a part of it and moving along with it**, as being dressed in a shirt, wearing a ring, or bearing armour. One kind belongs to the organism's constitution, as a cat's natural relation to its skin; another is accidental, as a person's relation to clothing. Broader ordinary language uses *having* for possession or control, as Zayd has a horse, the soul has powers, or a vessel has wine. Avicenna famously doubts whether this category has a properly determinable essence distinct from all other categories: **having quantity, quality, a relation, a location or a containing substance** all attract the common grammatical “has,” but not in one obviously univocal formal sense. Restricting the category to **a movable encompassing object**, such as garment, shoes or armour, may avoid the ambiguity, yet it remains uncertain that the resulting relation merits classification as an **ultimate category of being**.

**“Among them is acting (*an yafʿal*) and being-acted-upon (*an yanfaʿil*).”** Acting is the state of a producer **continuously affecting another**, as a heater **while heating**. Being-acted-upon is the receptive state's **continuous becoming affected**, as water **while becoming warm**. These categories must not be confused with the **completed state after change**, e.g. a mature tree's height, water's obtained temperature, a fabric's burnt condition, or a person's now standing or sitting: these belong to quantity, quality, position and the like. Nor are acting and being-acted-upon simply the **producer's settled capacity** before and after action, such as a fire's disposition to burn. Both admit opposed processes, such as heating/cooling and becoming-hot/becoming-cold, and varying degrees of intensity or rate.

Al-Rāzī and other investigators deny independent **external existence** to these two categories: if every external acting itself required another distinct actual **acting to actualize it**, an infinite regress of effects and acts would be contained between a producer and one product. The reply limits the categories to **continuous, nonabiding production and change**, not every act of creating or acquiring existence. Instantaneous production, including divine origination, is not itself a gradual state called *an yafʿal*, nor is every simple reception *an yanfaʿil*. Al-Fārābī describes the latter as **a thing progressively becoming different**—in substance by generation and corruption, in magnitude by increase and decrease, in quality by alteration, and in place by local motion. The corresponding *an yafʿal* is the producer's changing relation to the **successive portions of what is produced**, as a heater progressively causes successive stages of warming. Each kind of being-acted-upon has a corresponding kind of acting: building corresponds to being-built, demolition to being-demolished, heating to becoming-hot. Contrariety in one is mirrored by contrariety in the other.

Avicenna prefers the grammatical forms **“to be acting”** and **“to be undergoing”** to the more general nouns “action” and “affection,” because the latter may also name the **stable result after the movement ceases**. The category is properly the **uncompleted orientation toward a terminus**, whether of quantity, quality, position or another field, precisely **while the change continues**. This concludes the available electronic text of **Division III: Accidents** at printed **volume I, page 285**; the next division is **المقصد الرابع في الجواهر — Substances**.

title: Introduction: division of substance and the status of the subject
en:
**Source:** electronic vol. I, pp. 285–287; canonical source characters 695039–699008 (exclusive).

The definition of *substance* (*jawhar*) according to the theologians and the philosophers has already been given. This fourth objective is arranged as a preliminary discussion dealing with its division and related matters, followed by two articles: one concerning bodies and the other concerning incorporeal substances.

**Division according to the theologians.** Since substance denotes what is intrinsically spatially situated (*al-mutaḥayyiz bi-l-dhāt*), it either admits division—in which case it is a **body** (*jism*)—or does not, in which case it is the **indivisible substance** (*al-jawhar al-fard*).

**Division according to the Peripatetic philosophers.** Substance is either intellect (*ʿaql*), soul (*nafs*), body, prime matter (*hayūlā*), or form (*ṣūra*). They give several paths for obtaining this division. These proceed from their own doctrines: that no indivisible atom exists; that intellect and soul are immaterial; that the reality of body involves an inhering substance and another in which it inheres; and analogous principles. Without these assumptions their divisions are open to objections whose course is evident.

On the **first path**, a substance which inheres in another substance is a *form*. If it does not, but serves as the recipient or substrate of another substance, it is *matter*. If it is compounded of the inhering principle and its substrate, it is *body*. If it is none of these but has a relation to body by way of governance and management (*tadbīr wa-taṣarruf*), it is a *soul*. Otherwise it is an *intellect*.

On the **second path**, consider whether substance is separate in its very being (*mufāriq fī dhātih*), that is, independent of conjunction with another substance. If it is, and is also separate in its operation, it is intellect; if not separate in operation, it is soul. If it is not separate in its being but joined to another substance, it must inhere in that other, receive it as a substrate, or be compounded from the two. What were none of these would be separate rather than conjoined.

On the **third path**, what admits the three dimensions is a body. Otherwise, a constituent of body by which it is actual is form, while that by which it is potential is matter. Something which is not a constituent, but which directs and acts through body, is soul; otherwise intellect. This corresponds to the division in the *Shifāʾ*: if a substance is composite it is body; if simple, and entering into the constitution of a composite as wood enters the existence of a chair, it is matter; if entering as the chair's shape enters it, it is form. If it does not enter the composite but subsists separately, it is a soul if it has a relationship to bodies involving their movement and direction, otherwise intellect.

**Objection.** Body surely exists actually with prime matter as well, because matter cannot be separated from form, as will be explained. **Reply.** With respect to matter taken precisely as matter, the existence of the composite is potential; with respect to form it is actual. In the *Shifāʾ*, matter is that by regard to which the composite does not possess its rationally determinate actuality but has being potentially, whereas it is by the acquisition of form that the composite actually is what it is. So essential is form in this respect that, were form able to exist without matter, the actual attainment of the composite would follow from it.

**Second objection.** The form inhering in prime matter and entering the constitution of body is specifically corporeal form (*al-ṣūra al-jismiyya*). Specific substantial form (*al-ṣūra al-nawʿiyya*) has body itself for its recipient, even though this body may be called matter or *hayūlā* insofar as forms succeed one another in it. **Reply.** Though specific form does not enter the constitution of body *as such*, it does enter the constitution of its species, both celestial and elemental. It will also be shown that its recipient is prime matter.

According to some **ancient philosophers**, a substance which occupies a region is *corporeal*, namely body alone: they do not establish a distinct inhering substance called form and a recipient substance called prime matter. For them *matter* is a name for body as receptive of accidents determining different kinds of bodies, and *form* names those accidents. What is not spatially situated is *spiritual*, that is, soul or intellect.

### A terminological caution: *mawḍūʿ*, *maḥall*, *ḥāll*, and *ʿaraḍ*

The *subject* (*mawḍūʿ*) has already been defined as a recipient (*maḥall*) which constitutes or sustains what inheres in it (*al-ḥāll*). Thus every subject is a recipient, but not every recipient is a subject. What inheres may be a substance—such as a form—or an accident, so *inhering item* has a wider extension than *accident*. An accident does not subsist through itself, and therefore cannot supply another item's substance-constituting ground, although it can be the locus of another accident in the sense of a qualifying specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ nāʿit*). An accident and a subject are accordingly entirely disparate in extension; an accident and a recipient intersect partially: an accident may receive another accident, but some recipients are substances, while some accidents receive nothing.

**Objection.** An accident's dependence on a subject sustaining it is necessary; that is the meaning of *subject*. If an accident receives another accident, must it not therefore be a subject? **Reply.** The latter accident may depend upon the ultimate subject *through* an intervening accident, which is its immediate recipient and by which the first subject is qualified. Speed, for example, pertains to body through motion. From the fact that every accident ultimately depends upon a subject, it does not follow that the first locus by which it is specified must itself be a substantial subject.

### Do universals of substance need a subject?

The subject is that recipient on which the inhering thing depends for its constitution, whereas substance is what subsists through itself rather than through another. That a substance is not in a subject should therefore be plain. Yet a misunderstanding may suggest that this applies only to individual substances, not to their universal natures. It has two grounds. First, universal substances depend for their existence upon the individuals of which they are predicated, and those individuals are their *subjects*. Second, a universal nature exists as a form in a particular soul and cannot subsist *as universal* without it.

**Reply to the first.** This confuses two senses of *subject*: the subject of predication or judgement in a proposition, and the recipient that sustains an inhering reality. An individual is the subject of a universal in the first sense, not the second. **Reply to the second.** To call such forms substances means that, considered as natures in themselves, they are of a kind which, when existing outside the mind, does not exist in a subject. Considered instead under their actual inherence in an individual soul and dependence upon it, they are particular accidents—not universal substances.

**Editorial note.** This is a first-pass English translation of the specified opening interval, closely following the Arabic argument and its objections. The source is a 1981 electronic transcription, not an independently collated printed or manuscript witness. The chair example is illustrative of the distinction between matter and form and should not be taken as proof that chair-shape is itself a natural substantial form.

title: First article: the definition and nature of body
en:
**Source:** electronic vol. I, pp. 287–291; canonical source characters 699008–709974 (exclusive).

There is no obscurity or controversy in the fact that, in Arabic—as in its equivalents in other languages—the word *body* (*jism*) is applied to a single intelligible meaning, distinguishable from what is other than it. But because the reality of body is obscure and its concomitants are numerous, disagreement has arisen concerning the determination of its quiddity and the wording of its definition. This has even produced disagreements as to whether certain things count as bodies.

### Among the verifying theologians

In the view of the more exacting theologians, body is **a substance admitting division**, without restricting division to three spatial dimensions. If something were composed of two indivisible substances, the aggregate would be the body, not each one of the two. Al-Qāḍī [the source does not specify a full name at this point] held that each of those two was itself a body. His argument is: each is a *composed substance*; every composed substance is a body. The minor premise rests on the claim that a single accident of composition (*taʾlīf*) cannot subsist in two substrates; each part therefore has its own composition inhering in it, and is thereby composed.

The reply distinguishes attribution to an aggregate *as an aggregate* from attribution to each of its constituents. Composition is a relation between the two things; when considered with reference to the whole, it makes the whole a thing *composed of* things, and when considered with reference to each part, it makes that part a thing *composed with* another. The analogous terminological distinction appears in grammar between a composite utterance involving predication and an inflected expression as described in the text. Hence the body is composite in the former sense, and each part is composite only in the latter. The supposedly repeated middle term therefore changes its meaning.

**Objection.** The *taʾlīf* under consideration is a specific accident rather than the ordinary linguistic meaning of combination, which entails plurality. Among the Muʿtazila it is held to explain the difficulty of pulling constituent parts apart. **Reply.** One may simply deny the major premise that everything so composed must itself be a body.

Al-Āmidī treats the dispute as verbal, concerning what meaning the term *body* was instituted to designate. The author of *al-Mawāqif*, however, treats it as substantive: when the parts gather and there is a body, does there exist a special accident of composition or connection (*ittiṣāl*) responsible, as Muʿtazilites maintain, for the difficulty of separation? Or is body only the assembled parts themselves? On the latter reconstruction, al-Qāḍī affirms an accident of composition, but denies that one such accident inheres in both parts jointly; rather each part has its own, and so each becomes a body. He is then said to make the part analogous to matter and composition analogous to form. Al-Taftāzānī objects that the majority of the theologians also accept composition, without supposing one accident to inhere in two separate subjects. It is still worse to make the difference between al-Qāḍī and the Muʿtazila simply the latter's supposed affirmation of composition: al-Qāḍī himself affirms it, while the Muʿtazila do not say that two atoms suffice to form a body.

### The Muʿtazilite definition

Their familiar account calls body **that which is long, broad, and deep** (*al-ṭawīl al-ʿarīḍ al-ʿamīq*). They agree that this is not a strict essential definition (*ḥadd*) but a description by a distinctive property (*rasm bi-l-khāṣṣa*). Its being a *proper* characteristic rests partly on their not positing the mathematical body (*al-jism al-taʿlīmī*) which is the quantity of three dimensions. Were that accepted, dimensional extension would belong also to a quantity which is not a natural body, so they would have to add *substance* to the definition and thereby construct a characteristic of the natural body from an intrinsic and an extrinsic term, rather as one might describe a bat by flying and giving birth. That the term *substance* is generic does not prevent the description from being extrinsic when its other constituent is extrinsic. Alternatively, *long* may be meant as what has length as a possible or initial accident; this would exclude mathematical body because its dimensions are constituents of it.

**Objection from convertibility.** A distinctive characteristic is fit to define only if it is comprehensive and inseparable. This one is alleged to be neither. As to comprehensiveness, a sphere has no actual straight line, and an imagined infinite body lacks a bounding surface. Even if the existence of an infinite body is excluded by an independent demonstration, it can still be considered as body; unlike the putative case of four items without evenness, whose evenness is essential. As to inseparability, a particular piece of wax can be stretched from one measure of length and breadth to another while remaining the same body. Its original dimensions depart.

**Reply.** Deny, first, that the absence of a line or surface *actually* entails the absence of length, breadth and depth. What is meant is the body's **capacity** for the relevant dimensions; this capacity is universal and abiding. Furthermore, the change in measurement asserted in the wax example is not accepted by the theologians in that form: the indivisible substances constituting it are redistributed from length into breadth. Even if actual dimensional changes are conceded, dimensions *in general* persist, while only their particular measurements cease.

**Further objection.** If magnitudes are denied, length alone is a distinctive characteristic of body; if magnitudes are affirmed, being a *long substance* already suffices. Why add breadth and depth? **Reply.** That would be valid only if any divided or composed substance qualified as a body—even one compounded of two indivisibles. But the Muʿtazila do not maintain this. According to al-Naẓẓām, the constituents of each body are infinitely numerous; according to al-Jubbāʾī, the least number is eight, arranged in two layers of four; according to Abū al-Hudhayl, six, arranged three upon three; another position specifies four, in three different spatial directions. The proposed arrangement of three meeting as a triangle with another above the meeting-point is disputed because it would allegedly require their division. In short, an aggregate below the minimum number required for corporeality, or one arranged only in one direction (called a *line*) or in two (called a *surface*), falls between a fully-fledged body and an indivisible substance. Breadth and depth exclude these intermediate configurations.

### The philosophers' definition

The description just discussed was also used by earlier philosophers. Subsequent Peripatetics, and especially Aristotle and his followers, made the intended claim explicit. One must distinguish natural body from mathematical body, and one must not require dimensions to be actual. Hence they say: **body is a substance capable of the three dimensions**—that is, a substance within which three dimensions may be posited or supposed (*yumkin an yufraḍa fīhi abʿād thalātha*).

Some add that the three dimensions meet at **right angles**. A line standing upon another at right angles makes two equal angles; if inclined, it makes one acute and another obtuse. We may suppose a first dimension through body in any direction, a second intersecting it at right angles, and a third perpendicular to both. In the intended geometrical arrangement only one third perpendicular direction is available for the given first two. The qualification specifies the precise kind of three-dimensionality intended, even though other non-orthogonal dimensions can be projected through a body. The discussion in *al-Mawāqif* should thus be understood as asserting the possibility of perpendicular intersection, not the necessity of actual perpendicular lines. It also guards against mistakenly treating a surface—conceived by an atomist as a substantial array of atoms—as though it already met the definition of body. The mathematical body is not being silently identified with natural body.

The word **supposable** or **capable of being posited** is significant. Corporeality is not constituted by the body's particular dimensions *in act*. The dimensions may change without loss of corporeality, as in the wax example, and may increase or diminish through rarefaction and condensation. A body's essence is conceivable independently of actual surfaces and lines, as in the supposition of infinite body; a perfectly solid sphere likewise need not contain an actual line. Nor does the *exercise* of geometrical supposition have to occur: its **possibility** is sufficient. To posit the three dimensions in a separate immaterial substance is impossible in the relevant ontological sense, not merely difficult for imagination.

The philosophers take *possibility* here in its broad sense, encompassing bodies in which the dimensional conditions obtain necessarily and actually, those in which some actual measurements vary, and those in which the relevant linear dimensions are only potential. Yet the actual referent of the word *dimension* is not always handled consistently. Sometimes it denotes the extended quantitative continuum filling the body between surfaces—**mathematical body**, an accident distinct from unchanging substantial **corporeal form**. At other times it denotes actual or potential lines; elsewhere it seems to denote bounding lines or surfaces. The last cannot be literally identical with the three dimensions meeting at right angles. A preferable reading is **three supposable, intersecting directions of extension**, called length, breadth, and depth. These are not themselves three already existing lines, either in the natural body or in mathematical body. Their potentiality must not be confused with the body's actual substantial continuity, since it is division, not continuity, which is potential in the relevant contrast.

Ibn Sīnā distinguishes *dimension* (*buʿd*) from a definite magnitude (*miqdār*): a dimension is what lies between non-coinciding limits and is such that further limits of their kind can be imagined in it. Thus, between two supposed points there is a linear dimension even where no line is actually drawn; between two opposite supposed lines there is a surface-like dimension even where no separate surface exists. Length is accordingly not identical with an actual line, nor breadth with an actual surface. A line has length, but length may be without an actual line; likewise a surface has breadth, yet breadth need not be an actual surface.

**Al-Rāzī's objection concerning imagination.** One can suppose three dimensions in the imaginative faculty (*wahm*) too, yet it is not a body. **Reply.** The capacity intended is realized **in external existence**, as when 'moist' means that which admits shapes readily, not whatever the mind can arbitrarily conceive as doing so. In any case, the faculty of imagination does not qualify as a *substance* in the same sense merely by being imaginable. The possibility in question is the possibility of actual embodiment, not conceptual depiction alone.

**His objection concerning prime matter.** Prime matter can receive three dimensions, although only on condition that it receive corporeal form. If *form* itself is made part of the receiver, this seems to contradict the philosophers' distinction: form is the principle of actuality, whereas matter is the principle of receptivity and potentiality. **Reply.** What prime matter receives in its own right are forms, not quantitative and qualitative accidents as such; the philosophers expressly give it no proper share of magnitude. The reception of accidental extension belongs to the corporeal form, itself a substantial extension through which quantitative extension can be received. The proposed definition also employs *receptivity* broadly enough to encompass the actual possession of extension, even necessary possession. The objection may be stronger if directed against the corporeal form itself, depending on how its reception of further dimensions is construed.

### Is the definition a true *ḥadd* or only a *rasm*?

Al-Taftāzānī's more apparent judgment is that this definition is a **description through a composite proper characteristic**, not a real essential definition. Even supposing *substance* is a genus, 'receptive of dimensions' is not related to that genus exactly as an essential differentia should be. The body's being constituted by merely imagined dimensions is difficult to understand. The claim that body is externally compounded of matter and form, not of 'substance' and 'receptive of dimensions', cannot itself settle this, because one must distinguish **external constituents** from **intelligible essential parts** or definitions.

A passage reported from Ibn Sīnā itself suggests hesitation between *ḥadd* and *rasm*. Al-Rāzī denies that it can be a real definition: (1) *substance* cannot serve as its genus, and (2) the capacity for dimensions cannot serve as its differentia. First, *substance* defined as 'what exists not in a subject' includes 'exists', which, if existence is additional to quiddity, is not an essential ingredient of the thing defined but a second intelligible. The absence of a need for a subject is negative, and as such seems unsuitable as an intrinsic constituent of a real essence. This does not entail that all ordinary natural universals are second logical intentions: one must separate logical from natural universals.

Another argument against *substance* as a genus says that, if it were a true genus, substances would have to differ by specific differences. If those differences themselves counted as substances, regress would follow; if they were accidents, substance would be constituted by accident. That would both undermine its independence of a subject and make an accident predicable essentially of the substance, as differentia is predicated of species.

**Source:** electronic vol. I, pp. 291–292; canonical source characters 709974–711794 (exclusive).

In setting out the different doctrines concerning the reality of body, the authorities have proposed a division based on **simple body**, namely one not composed of bodies of unlike natures. Its possible divisions either are actual or are not all actual; in either case they are finite or infinite. On this fourfold scheme: the first view belongs to the theologians, the second to al-Naẓẓām, the third to most philosophers, and the fourth to Muḥammad al-Shahrastānī. Yet the mere denial that *all* divisions are already actual leaves room for the view that **some** are actual. Democritus is said to hold that bodies comprise small, solid parts which admit division in the imagination but not in actuality. Therefore the source distinguishes **five**, rather than only four, possibilities.

The doctrine that a body consists of surfaces, surfaces of lines, and lines of points conceived as indivisible substances is treated as a variant of theologians' atomism which requires extension in three directions and denies corporeality to fewer than eight constituents. Among philosophers accepting indefinite divisibility, some also make the possibility of division dependent upon prime matter; others reject this dependence. The view attributed to al-Najjār and Ḍirār, that body is composed *entirely of accidents*—colours, tastes, smells, and the like—is dismissed as manifestly false.

The three principal doctrines worthy of extended consideration are these. **(1) The theologians:** body is constituted by finitely many indivisible substances. **(2) The Peripatetics:** body is compounded from prime matter and substantial form. **(3) The Illuminationists:** body in itself is simple, as it appears to the senses; it does not consist of separately existing constituents, yet it has in its own nature a capacity for division which does not terminate in an absolutely indivisible limit, just as divine power has no such ultimate limit in its possible objects.

There is thus something like agreement among the schools that there is a **subject for the successive reception of forms and accidents**, though they interpret it very differently. For the Illuminationists this is body itself: insofar as it receives magnitudes it may be called matter or prime matter, while the magnitudes inhering in it may be called forms. For the Peripatetics it is a substance constituted through another substance inhering in it; their union constitutes a body receptive of quantities and other accidents. For the theologians it consists of indivisible substances which acquire the accident of composition, thereby making a body. Their composition plays a role *analogous* to the Peripatetic form, but it remains an **accident** subsisting only in its recipient, whereas the philosophers' form is a substance, and it is also that through which its recipient—prime matter—is constituted as the actual compound.

**Editorial note.** This section is the opening taxonomy of theories, not yet the subsequent extended demonstrations for or against atoms, hylomorphism, or substantial continuity. The source's classifications of Democritus and Illuminationist doctrine require independent historical comparison before being attributed as settled facts about those authors.

title: The third investigation: the indivisible part, first route

**Source:** *Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid*, digital I.292–293, source characters 711794–714769 (exclusive). **Status:** new close working translation; electronic reading uncollated with print.

The theologians have **two routes** for establishing that a body consists of parts which admit of no further division. The **first** is to prove that susceptibility to division entails that the divisions already exist [as distinguishable parts]. Its formulation is this: every body is susceptible to division—this is conceded—and everything susceptible to division has its parts actually present. Several arguments are offered for the latter claim.

**First argument.** If what admits division were not already divided in actuality, but were one in itself, as it seems to sense-perception, then *unity itself* would admit division. The consequence is false, because unity means precisely the absence of division. The alleged entailment follows because unity, on this supposition, is an attribute inhering in the divisible subject, whether necessary to it or not: unity is neither that subject itself nor one of its parts. When the subject is divided, what inheres in it must be divided, since that which inheres in one portion is not what inheres in another. **Reply:** Unity belongs to the mind's considerations (*iʿtibārāt ʿaqliyya*). Even if it is conceded to be an attribute, it is not one of the pervasive (*sāriya*) accidents whose extension is divided by the division of the subject.

**Second argument.** Were body originally a single [undivided] entity, dividing it and separating its parts would annihilate it, since the operation removes one numerical identity and produces two others. But this consequence is plainly false: the prick of a mosquito's needle through the sea does not annihilate a sea and bring two new seas into existence. **Reply:** If “sea” means that water **together with its continuity**, then its uninterrupted continuity is indeed lost upon separation. If “sea” means the water itself, with continuity left out of consideration, no sea has been annihilated and no two seas have been newly produced. This fits the philosophers' principle that the recipient of a determination must remain when the determination is received, coexisting with it.

One may transfer the question to **matter**. If matter comprises several actually distinct parts, the atomists obtain their result.
