title: Second route: the indivisible substance, points, motion and time
en:
**Source:** digital I.293–296, characters 714769–720479 (exclusive). **Status:** new close working translation; print collation pending.

**The second route** taken by the theologians is to establish the occurrence within body of a **substance that does not admit division at all**—not by cutting, breaking, imagining, or intellectual supposition. Cutting employs a penetrating instrument whereas breaking need not; both bring about physical separation. Imaginary division and intellectual supposition need not do so. Imagination, understood as the operation of the estimative faculty governing the bodily senses, may stop at a finite sequence of divisions because bodily powers have limited acts. By contrast, intellect can think universally of the small and the great, the finite and the infinite, and can continue a merely supposed division.

**Objection:** The existence of an indivisible substance does not yet show that **bodies are composed** from such substances. **Reply:** Granted, but it suffices to refute the philosophers' argument that an indivisible substance is impossible. Some demonstrations additionally purport to establish the composition itself.

The methods used in this second route include arguments which themselves assume that a body's capacity for division requires actually present portions.

**First:** God can replace the cohesion of a body's parts with their complete separation. His power relates equally to the two contrary states. Once all conjunction has ceased, there must be a part incapable of further subdivision: if every part were still divisible, a conjunction would remain [between its subordinate portions]. The issue is whether the premise of **complete actual separation** is coherent without already presupposing the atomist thesis.

**Second:** Without indivisible parts a mountain would not be greater than a mustard seed. Each would admit infinitely many divisions, thus each would have infinitely many constituent parts without numerical excess, and this is said to amount to equality. **Objection:** Even if they had equally infinite numbers of parts, their **magnitudes** could still differ. **Reply alleged by the atomists:** Magnitude differs according to the number of parts; the greater body must have more parts. A variant argument says that, were both divisible without limit, one could separate enough layers from the mustard seed to cover both surfaces of the heavens and fill the interval between them. The absurdity is evident. **Philosophical reply:** Unlimited divisibility does not mean that an infinite collection of divisions can be actualised and all separated. There is no inference from the former to an infinite number of actually separable layers.

**Third:** If division never reached something unextended and indivisible, even the extension of a mustard seed would be infinite in magnitude because it would be built up from infinitely many extensions.

A second family of arguments derives from describing **motion** as successive occurrences without permanence and **time** as a succession of indivisible moments. Movement over a distance is undeniable. But neither its past, which existed when present, nor its future, which will exist when present, exists **now**. Only what is present exists now; and the present of something whose essence is non-enduring cannot be divided into earlier and later portions, since the complete movement would then not be present. Alternatively, if the present motion had simultaneous divisible components, motion would be something of enduring or permanent existence (*qārr al-dhāt*). Therefore motion consists of indivisible present elements. Since motion corresponds to distance, with each portion of movement corresponding to a portion of distance, an indivisible movement demands a corresponding indivisible portion of distance. As one present moment passes and another succeeds it, motion is, on this account, composed of indivisible units, and the traversed distance likewise.

The argument can be sharpened through **time**, whose non-enduring character seems even more obvious than that of motion. The present of time cannot be subdivided even by intellectual supposition, it is argued, since to suppose a part other than a part would introduce an earlier and later within what is wholly present. Time corresponds to motion, which corresponds to distance; hence all three appear atomically partitioned. **The philosophers reject the premise:** They deny the existence of an independently standing indivisible *present* of time. Motion, in the relevant sense, is the **being-between** the starting point and the terminus; both time and motion have divisibility analogous to that of a body. This is a report of the competing position, not an admission that the atomist inference is established.

A third family of arguments begins from the contention that **the subject of a point** must be a substance without division.

**First:** The point exists: it is the extremity of an existing line; existing lines meet *at* something, not at sheer nonbeing; and a point has position, being indicated as *there*. Either the point is itself a substance or it is an accident. If an accident, it needs a substantial subject, directly or through a mediating accident according as one rejects or accepts the inherence of an accident in another accident. That substantial subject cannot be divisible, the argument says, or the point inhering in it would be divided. Either way an indivisible substance has been obtained.

**Second:** Place a genuine sphere upon a genuine plane. The sphere contacts it by something indivisible, for otherwise a straight line or flat surface would be found on the spherical surface and it would not be a sphere. This indivisible contact is either a substance, or an accident requiring an indivisible substantial subject. By rolling the sphere over the plane, one allegedly demonstrates that its spherical surface is composed of indivisible points. To deny the possible existence of a true sphere or plane or their contact is, the atomists say, a rejection of the philosophers' own foundations.

**Third:** If a line stands upon another line at one side of it, it meets the second through something indivisible. As the first moves across the second, the second line is shown to contain a succession of such indivisibles: that upon which the indivisible rests must itself be indivisible.

**Fourth:** Euclid demonstrates, it is argued, that the angle made by a straight line tangent to a circular circumference is the least possible angle. That angle cannot be divided, since otherwise half of it would be a smaller angle. The indivisible in question must be a substance or an accident inhering in one.

The philosophers distinguish here between **pervasive inherence**, as whiteness pervades a body, and **terminative inherence**, as a point is the end of a line, a line the boundary of a surface, and a surface the boundary of a mathematical body. Only the former must be divided with its subject; a point does not spread through the line like a quality. Al-Taftāzānī judges the sphere-and-plane case forceful, maintaining that the contact of their substances is necessary; he argues that to make the point of contact divisible even by supposition would destroy the sphere's genuinely spherical shape or replace it by a faceted one when contact changes. He also presses that the philosophers' point is only the **end of a line**, not an actually existing part of the sphere in its own right.

**Editorial qualification:** The arguments must remain recognisable as medieval geometrical and physical demonstrations; this working translation does not validate their premises by modern mathematics. The distinction of the existent point from the actual **component** of a body must not be suppressed.

title: Finitely many parts, interpenetration and the leap; reconstruction of al-Naẓẓām
en:
**Source:** digital I.296–298, source characters 720479–726819 (exclusive). **Status:** new source-ordered close explanatory translation; print collation pending.

**“They argued.”** Those who posit indivisible parts offer several arguments that a body's parts must be **finite in number**, contrary to the view attributed to al-Naẓẓām.

**First**, the parts are bounded between two limits. Anything enclosed by boundaries, whether counted or measured, must be finite. **Second**, infinitely many parts would make it impossible for a moving thing to reach the end of a distance. It would first have to cross half, then half of the remaining half, and so without end; an infinite completion of tasks seems impossible in finite time. One may recast this by saying that an infinite number of spatial portions entails infinitely many portions of motion, and these entail infinitely many portions of time. **Third**, a fast mover could never catch a slower mover who had a head start: upon the faster mover's traversing a unit, the slower would have traversed some unit, with no smaller unit available on the atomist assumption. Sensation and argument exclude intervening rests. Introducing a slower moving body rather than an unmoving one makes the objection specifically about overtaking; otherwise it reduces to the preceding argument about reaching a terminus. Al-Taftāzānī remarks that this overtaking difficulty can arise even if the number of parts is **finite**, and that the first three arguments address an infinite number of divisions **within every possible extension** and between any chosen boundaries. If the infinity is ascribed only to the totality of dimensions taken together, the argument needs an additional demonstration that the dimensions themselves are finite in number.

**Fourth**, suppose that eight indivisible parts make a composite having length, breadth and depth along three mutually perpendicular directions. That is already a body, and its number of parts is finite. To infer the finitude of parts in every finitely extended body, compare its magnitude with that of this constructed body: the ratio of one finite magnitude to another is finite, and, according to the argument, the ratio of magnitudes follows the ratio of constituent parts. If one magnitude contained infinitely many components, this would require an impossible ratio of finite to infinite. **Objection:** Al-Naẓẓām may deny that an atom ever exists independently; all such parts are components of a body and each body has infinitely many of them. **Reply:** The thought experiment selects eight constituents *within* a body, not eight separately subsisting atoms. **Fifth**, if magnitude tracks the number of its parts, then infinitely many parts in every body would imply that every body has infinite magnitude, which is manifestly false.

The familiar replies attributed to defenders of an infinity of parts are two. The first is **interpenetration** (*tadākhul*): one part penetrates the other completely, so that their occupied spaces are one. Adding parts need not then increase volume, and one need not correlate every spatial part with an additional part of motion and time. The second is **the leap** (*ṭafra*): the moving thing leaves one spatial position and comes to another without contacting or confronting what intervenes. Some positions of the route are traversed without the mover's encountering their parts; one therefore need not deny that it reaches an end or overtakes the slower mover.

Both answers are rejected. Total interpenetration equates a whole with its part in magnitude. A leap seems to amount to crossing a space **without movement through that space**. As an empirical illustration, a pen drawn across the page leaves a continuous black line without intervening white points. If the number of points jumped over were infinitely greater than the contacted points, the supposed unmarked portions ought to be perceptible. The claim that they have merely been mixed beyond the senses is therefore, the text argues, insufficient. Interpenetration is also criticised by considering a middle atom between two outer atoms. If the middle atom coincided entirely with both, it would not block their contact; and if every part coincided wholly, there would be no increase in extension and no extended body. Partial interpenetration, on the other hand, requires a portion of each atom to meet a portion of another and so reintroduces divisibility at least by supposition.

**An important correction of attribution follows.** Al-Naẓẓām did not, al-Taftāzānī says, begin by maintaining a theory that bodies are actually composed of an infinite number of atoms. Rather, while accepting the existence of a part, he examined the familiar arguments against its indivisibility, especially those which seem to contradict evident sensible phenomena, such as the disintegration of a millstone. He was driven to the assertion that every part admits limitless division. Because he additionally took the actual existence of divisions to follow from divisibility, the infinity of actual parts followed; to preserve movement and overtaking he resorted to the leap. Hence the polemical formulas “the leap of al-Naẓẓām” and “the theologians' breaking millstone.”

**Objection from the Muʿtazilite sources:** Al-Naẓẓām is reported to maintain that a body comprises colour, taste, smell and similar **accidents**. **Reply:** For him these are **substances**, not accidents. A useful reconstruction from the school's books separates ordinary states such as positional accidents, beliefs, pains and pleasures, which do not constitute the body, from colours, lights, tastes, smells, sounds and tactile qualities such as heat and cold, which al-Naẓẓām counts as substances or even subtle **bodies**. He makes a specific colour or quality a subtle body composed of joined substances. Their combination and interpenetration produce the gross body we call an inanimate object; spirit too is a subtle body regarded as one thing, while animate beings are of one genus. Most theologians, by contrast, treat all those sensible qualities as accidents. Dirār b. ʿAmr and al-Ḥusayn al-Najjār describe the body as a collection of such accidents, whereas other theologians describe it as substances in which accidents inhere.

Al-Taftāzānī therefore questions *al-Mawāqif*'s attribution of the doctrine that body is a collection of accidents to al-Naẓẓām and al-Najjār; he suggests **Dirār** should be named instead of al-Naẓẓām, as in other books. He then supplies a possible defence of *al-Mawāqif*: if the common subject is the spatially extended thing whose three dimensions all agree upon, al-Naẓẓām constructs it out of colour, taste and smell, things which the others classify as accidents, **although he himself calls them substances or bodies**. In that sense he agrees with al-Najjār in the account of the body's constitution while differing in nomenclature.

But the arguments against both cannot be transferred uncritically. For al-Naẓẓām, blackness itself, for example, is an independently existing subtle body made of similar substances; its components need not resemble those of sweetness or heat. The assertion that accidents must inhere in something other than themselves therefore misses his claim, as may the assertion that bodies endure while accidents do not, since he does not concede the endurance of bodies. A merely dialectical denial that all substances have the same nature is not a substantive answer for a defender of the homogeneous-substance thesis. The better reply within that school, al-Taftāzānī proposes, is to deny that bodies differ **in their very essences**, attributing their differences to accidents established by the will of an agent who acts through choice.

An additional difficulty is raised against making a set of **non-enduring accidents constituent parts of an enduring body**: the disappearance of the parts would entail the disappearance of the whole. The opponent might instead say “substances persist,” but this can equivocate between an indivisible substance and an aggregate body. The source here deliberately distinguishes the durability of the **elements** from the alleged durability of their **composite**.

**Editorial note:** This segment ends just before the new discussion beginning “Crossing the infinite in a finite [time] is error.” The corrected attribution to Dirār, and the difference between a substance *named* by al-Naẓẓām and an accident *as analysed by his opponents*, are vital for accurate comparison with later discussions of body and sensible qualities.

title: Traversing infinitely divisible distance; the philosophers' first arguments against atoms
en:
**Source:** digital I.298–300, canonical characters 726819–730237 (exclusive). **Status:** new close explanatory draft.

**“To traverse an infinity in a finite interval is error.”** One might answer the objection that no body could traverse a finite distance consisting of infinitely many parts by matching each such part of space with a part of motion and a part of time. These divisions do not make the elapsed time infinite in magnitude; a finite interval of time, like a finite body, may permit infinitely many divisions. According to the philosophers this is exactly why traversing half the distance, half the remaining distance and so on does not prevent passage across a finite distance: the corresponding motion and time are **infinitely divisible**, but neither contains a completed infinity of actual successive stages.

The theologian's response is that **what actually comes into existence piece by piece from beginning to end** cannot have infinitely many successive actual members; the denial is judged obvious to reason. This is distinct from a merely **possible**, indefinitely continuing act of subdivision, which is precisely how the philosophers mean unlimited divisibility. **Objection:** Has the argument simply reverted to the first proof from what is bounded by two limits? **Reply:** Yes, but because the inference appears particularly evident for things extended in only one direction—movement and time—the same principle is applied to three-dimensional body.

**“As for the philosophers.”** Al-Taftāzānī now groups their numerous arguments **against** the indivisible atom according to the underlying premises. The first group assumes that the multiplication of a thing's **directions, sides or extremities** entails division of the thing itself.

**First:** A spatial atom, if real, must have distinguishable directions and sides. What in it is toward the right is other than what is toward the left, and likewise above versus below and front versus rear. The alleged indivisible substance would therefore be divided, a contradiction.

**Second:** When one atom is placed next to another, either they meet **entirely** or only through a part. If their entire occupied places coincide, two atoms fill no more space than one; the juxtaposition of atoms can never build volume and body. If they meet through some aspect rather than all, each has distinct extremities and is divisible.

**Third:** When three atoms are arranged in a row, the middle one either prevents the outer two from touching—so its contact with one differs from its contact with the other and the middle one is divided—or does not prevent contact, so that their juxtaposition produces no increased magnitude. The argument extends to any number of atoms.

**Fourth:** Imagine a sheet made of indivisible atoms, extending in length and breadth but not in thickness. When sunlight falls upon it, the illuminated face turned toward the sun differs from the opposite face; hence each supposed indivisible atom has distinguishable faces and divides.

**Fifth:** If a third indivisible atom occupies the joint between two touching atoms, it must meet the two **through different portions**, since if the entire third atom contacted only one it would rest upon that one rather than occupy their joint. The supposed phenomenon can be illustrated by placing an atom at a joint, by moving one atom from a first to a second position so that it crosses their boundary, by moving atoms from opposite ends of a four-atom line at equal speeds until they meet at the joint between the middle two, or by moving two atoms from ends of a five-atom line so that they meet above the middle atom. In each case one must assign different contacts to distinguishable portions of an allegedly indivisible atom.

Al-Taftāzānī notes **conditions required for these examples**. Some assume that an indivisible atom can exist by itself and move in any direction, including the specific curved motions used in the thought experiment. This does not follow from every atomist theory. A Muʿtazilite answer that the atom cannot be divided **actually** although it may be divided **in imagination** is, he says, a reversion toward the doctrine attributed to Democritus, not the strict denial of every conceivable division at issue here. These objections, therefore, require finer discrimination between **physical separation, imagined distinction, and genuine part-whole composition**.

title: Speed, intermittent rest, Euclidean geometry and proposed limits of atomism
en:
**Source:** digital I.300–303, canonical characters 730237–737598 (exclusive). **Status:** new source-ordered close explanatory rendering; printed source needs checking.

**“And another [route].”** A second philosophical route against the indivisible atom relies on differences between movements in **speed and slowness**. It assumes that the slower movement is not simply the faster movement broken up by intervals of **rest**. Some argue that an alternation of rest and movement is impossible in itself; others appeal to consequences judged plainly false: the instantaneous disintegration and rejoining of a rigid body; a complete cause existing without its effect; or an effect occurring without the motion needed to produce it.

Two movers may begin and end their movements together yet traverse different distances. The one that has covered more is faster. Were distance built from equal indivisibles, when the faster traversed one atom the slower would traverse **one**, making them equal, or **more**, making it faster, or **less**, dividing an indivisible atom. Only intermittent rests in the slower motion appear to remain. The theologians admit such rests in principle, so philosophers devise examples in which they would entail what sense and reason reject.

Among the cases are a **stone** whose component atoms must repeatedly separate and reconvene although it is paradigmatically solid; a tool like a **compass** whose separated parts would scatter; a **human body** which, on the theologians' own account, cannot keep its life and intentional motion while its parts separate; and a **celestial sphere**, whose internal dissolution some natural philosophers deny outright. Two further cases concern the causal timing of movements. If the sun moves but its shadow alternately rests, the alleged complete cause is present while its effect is absent. If a bucket is moved up a well while the hook that pulls it is intermittently at rest, the alleged effect occurs without its complete moving cause.

The bucket illustration is made exact. Take a well one hundred cubits deep; halfway down fasten one end of a fifty-cubit rope to a beam, and attach a bucket to the other end. A second fifty-cubit cord has a **hook** which engages the lower end of the first cord. Pulling the hook from the midpoint to the mouth of the well raises it fifty cubits while the bucket rises a full hundred. Their motions begin and end together; the hook's motion participates in the complete cause of the bucket's motion. If the hook's motion includes intermittent rests while the bucket's does not, the effect is said to continue without its required cause.

**Geometrical arguments** form a third route. The propositions are derived from Euclid, whose proofs assume the continuous divisibility of line and figure that strict atomism denies. Al-Taftāzānī therefore marks the danger of simply importing these demonstrations without showing that their constructions are possible for an opponent who rejects that assumption.

**First**, an **equilateral triangle** can be erected on any given straight line. If a line consists of only two indivisible parts, construction requires the apex or intersecting component to fall at a joint; an atom resting at the joint would itself have to be divisible. **Second**, **every angle can be bisected**; where its vertex is atomic, the division threatens to divide the atomic vertex. **Third**, every **straight line can be bisected**: a line composed of an odd number of indivisible parts would require halving the middle part. The geometric construction can be made through a pair of equilateral triangles erected on opposite sides of the line and joining their vertices, or by constructing a triangle through two equal circles centred on the endpoints. But the construction of the **circle** itself is unavailable without further argument against the atomist.

**Fourth**, the **circle and sphere** appear not merely conceivable but actual. A finite line rotating about one fixed endpoint traces a circle, and a semicircle rotated about its diameter traces a sphere. The distance of every point of a circle's circumference from its centre, and similarly of a sphere's surface from its centre, is equal. Such geometrical figures are argued to contradict indivisible atomic constituents. If atoms make up a circle, either their outer and inner surfaces meet their neighbours in the same way, or they do not. If the outer exposed faces are larger than the inner faces, an atom is divisible. If both are equal, then inner and outer circular boundaries have equal total length; this would absurdly equate a small circle near the centre with the largest possible enclosing circle. If outer faces have gaps, the gaps must either admit an indivisible atom—making the outer circumference disproportionately larger than the inner—or be smaller than an atom, again dividing it. Likewise, a sphere's successive circles of latitude cannot all possess the same **number of indivisible parts** from equator to pole, nor can their lengths differ by less than one such part.

The philosophical inference is: if genuine circles and spheres are possible, the indivisible atom is not. **Al-Taftāzānī's caution:** Making a line or semicircle rotate in precisely the required manner is here a **thought construction**; such a mental picture is not yet a proof of the existence or possibility of what it depicts. If line and surface really were atomic, the proposed continuous rotation would be barred under its own assumptions. Therefore it is circular to assume the very continuity whose denial is under dispute.

**Fifth**, the Euclidean **Pythagorean theorem** (called the *bridal figure*, *shakl al-ʿarūs*) says that in a right-angled triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the combined squares on the other sides. If each leg is ten units, the hypotenuse has length √200, strictly between fourteen and fifteen units. If no fractional part of an atom is available, how can that length be composed? The same problem arises whenever the sum of the squares of the legs is not a perfect square.

**Sixth**, two perpendicular lines each made of one or two indivisible units would have a hypotenuse **larger than each leg and smaller than their sum**. That demands a measure between integral atomic lengths. **Seventh**, for a square drawn as tightly as possible using four atomic units on each side, the diagonal either contains contacting atoms and becomes equal to the side, contrary to the theorem, or contains gaps. If the gaps fit atoms, the diagonal grows too large; if they are smaller than atoms, strict indivisibility is abandoned. This yields variations of the demonstration traditionally called the *ass's bridge* (*shakl al-ḥimārī*) alongside the bridal figure.

Another group of arguments relies on premises **open to denial**. **First**, were a body composed of atoms, those parts would be **essential components** of bodyhood and therefore intelligible whenever the nature of body is grasped. **Reply:** Only the status of conceptual components such as genus and differentia follows automatically from a complete grasp of an essence; even they may be initially unknown when an essence is not completely understood. External constituents may certainly require investigation: the philosophers themselves disagree about matter and substantial form, although they call these constituents of bodies. **Second**, an atom, being finite, would have a **figure**, whether spherical or polygonal, and either figure seems divisible. In particular spheres assembled together leave gaps smaller than one sphere. **Reply:** The need for a definite figure and the consequences of sphere-packing have not been established for an indivisible spatial **part** merely because they apply to macroscopic spherical bodies. **Third**, every body at some moment casts a shadow twice its length; hence half the shadow corresponds to half the body. Applied to a body of an odd number of atomic units, a half-length divides an atom. **Reply:** The universal proposition is denied; the construction works only where the body admits a half in the relevant sense.

**Editorial conclusion:** The investigation so far is a sustained dialectic, not a straightforward list of proofs endorsed without qualification. Arguments for atoms sometimes assume that possible division yields actually present parts; arguments against atoms often assume geometrical continuity before establishing it. The next section turns to the doctrine of Democritus and related theories of minute bodies. The current interval ends immediately before **قال ثم إنهم أبطلوا**.

title: Democritean minute bodies and the several senses of division
en:
**Source:** digital I.303–304, canonical characters 737598–740552 (exclusive). **Status:** source-ordered working English, uncollated.

**“Then they refuted [another doctrine].”** The reference is to Democritus and certain ancient philosophers. On their account, what we see as a homogeneous body, water for example, is not absolutely simple. It arises from the **contact** of minute homogeneous bodies, maximally hard, which do not admit of **separative division** (*qisma infikākiyya*) but can be divided in thought or imagination. This view differs from strict indivisible-substance atomism in **calling its primitives bodies** and accepting at least **conceptual division** within them.

The argument against it proceeds from the sameness of nature attributed to these ultimate bodies. What is possible for any one, or for the composite produced through their contact, should be possible for another of the same nature. Separative division is possible for the composite. If division were intrinsically impossible for the primitive, it would also be impossible for the composite built from primitives having the same nature. That a primitive cannot **actually** be broken apart because of its particular identity, extreme smallness, great hardness, species-form, or the absence of a suitably sharp instrument does not prove that breakability is impossible for its **common bodily nature**.

Al-Rāzī objects that the individual extensions by which bodies are characterised **pass away upon separation** and new ones arise upon conjunction; perhaps their distinctive individuating identity blocks breakability. Al-Taftāzānī replies that this contingent impediment does not defeat an argument about the **possibility arising from the nature itself**. Another objection denies that all bodies share one essence. A proposed defender of Democritus might hold that each primitive has an essentially different nature, and thus deny the transfer of possibility of separation from the composite to its constituents. If no two bodies shared an essence, the general argument for **prime matter** would indeed fail. But it is implausible to apply such heterogeneity to what is presented as a **homogeneous, simple body**. One should not universalise from a mixed body to bodies whose natures may differ.

A further formula says that division produces two portions whose **natures** equal that of the original whole. This should be restricted to division of a homogeneous body. “Nature” in this discussion means the primary source of an essential property of a thing, whether movement, rest or another act, a sense broader than physical *ṭabīʿa* narrowly understood.

Several kinds of division must be distinguished. There is **physical separation** by breaking or cutting; **imagined or intellectually supposed division**; and a division obtained by distinguishing different attributes, whether **intrinsic and enduring** in the subject such as black and white, or **relational** such as contact and alignment. If the distinction in attributes does not cause physical severance, a body partially heated, partially illuminated, or touching another body through one region has **not** thereby become two bodies in external existence. When the heating, illumination or contact ceases, the feature by which the portions were distinguished ceases. Were this a genuine external separation, a traveller passing successive boundaries of a continuous path would successively divide the path into actually independent pieces and reunite it whenever travel ceased.

It is true that the region bearing whiteness is not identical **under that attribution** with the region bearing blackness. But the otherness belongs to the consideration of the attributes and the resulting intellectual supposition, not to a rupture of the body's substantial continuity. The *Shifāʾ* allows division by the **supposed assignment** of an attribute to only part of a body: when the attribute disappears the relevant subdivision also disappears. Consequently, when the *Sharḥ al-Ishārāt* speaks of a real distinction arising from two attributes without physical separation, it may mean a distinction **founded on an external circumstance**, not that the body is externally cut into two. When the logic of the *Shifāʾ* calls this a division “in act,” its “act” can refer to the activity of **intellect**, not a separate actualisation of external pieces.

**Editorial significance:** The distinction between *in actuality as a conceptually founded attribution* and *actually existing, externally separate constituents* is decisive. The dispute between Democritus and the strict kalām atomist should not be reduced to a mere difference over the size of atoms.

title: The Peripatetic proof of matter and corporeal form: presentation and five difficulties
en:
**Source:** digital I.304–307, canonical characters 740552–748826 (exclusive). **Status:** newly drafted source-ordered close explanatory English; printed-source collation outstanding.

**“Then the Peripatetics argued.”** Once one rejects a body composed of indivisible constituents, whether wholly indivisible or indivisible only against physical cutting, body seems to be **one continuous thing in itself**, as sense perceives it, although **susceptible to separation**. The philosophers therefore distinguish an **intrinsic substantial extension** from its variable **accidental magnitude**, the latter being *mathematical body*. A lump of wax may be shaped into a sphere, a cube, or a thin sheet, with its dimensions varying, while some bodily constituent persists. The philosophers maintain that without grasping a substantially extended nature one cannot grasp body at all; indeed, the first feature grasped is a substance having dimensions in different directions.

Plato and his adherents treat this substantially extended nature as **the body itself**, capable by its nature of separation. Aristotle and his adherents take it to be a **part** of body—the constituent which inheres in **another constituent** capable of receiving the contrary states of continuity and discontinuity. A recipient must remain while the opposed determination is received. Since the same continuous unity cannot itself remain unchanged when it is broken, a body must have a distinct **substratum** which persists while different individual instances of continuity come and go. That substratum is called **matter** (*hayūlā*); the informing substantial constituent is **corporeal form** (*ṣūra jismiyya*).

The initial presentation requires precision. What we first apprehend is a substantial **extended identity** which does not perish merely because its particular measurements change. The philosophers often call it *ittiṣāl* or the continuous, meaning **that substance whose nature is to be continuous**, not merely an accidental bond. “Continuity,” however, has several other senses. It may be a relation, such as a body moving jointly with another or two magnitudes joining at a common boundary as the sides of an angle do. It may be a nonrelational **quantitative character**: the possibility of a supposed division producing a **common boundary**, which is the end of either portion, such as a surface between portions of a body, a line between portions of a surface, or a point between portions of a line. This sense of continuity distinguishes **continuous magnitude** from **discrete number**. Mathematical body is continuous in this quantitative sense; corporeal form is continuous in the sense that mathematical extension is possible in it; and the natural body is continuous insofar as corporeal form belongs to it. These meanings must not be collapsed.

The substantially continuous identity, the argument continues, does **not** persist as the same individual continuity when separation occurs: one continuity is abolished and two replace it. Yet common experience recognises something remaining in both states. The difference is evident between (a) one entity's being totally annihilated and two unrelated new entities produced, and (b) one body becoming two by separation; likewise between two things disappearing and a new third being created, and two bodies becoming one by conjunction. Water poured from a jar into several cups is divided but not destroyed and newly created as water; water returned from several cups into a jar is joined. The **persisting recipient** is called **prime matter**, which in itself is pure capacity, neither already one and continuous nor already many and disconnected. Its apparent unity is through the continuity of a form, and its multiplicity through the opposed states that subsequently occur.

**Objection:** Some theologians and philosophers reject this putative **substantial extension**. Why should it be the *first thing understood* about body, instead of ordinary spatial dimensions and intelligible measurements? **Reply:** No school denies, according to the author, a substantial corporeal thing whose nature allows extension and continuity and which can be apprehended by sense at least through its accidents. The issue is whether that corporeal thing is intrinsically a **single continuous reality** or a composite of parts, and if continuous whether it constitutes the **entire** body or needs another constituent. Some theologians and philosophers reject **accidental quantities** as positive entities on the ground that a surface is merely the body's limit, a line the surface's limit and a point the line's limit. That question must not be confused with the existence of a substantial extended body.

**First difficulty:** Continuity cannot be a substance or a substantial part, for what it means is the contrary of separation, both seemingly alternating accidents of body reducible to unity and plurality. **Reply:** Substantial continuity here means **the substance naturally apt for extension**; it does not mean the fleeting contrary of separation. Whether this nature is externally one or composed, and whether it is a full body or only a part, is what requires proof. **Counter-objection:** Even if this substantially extended subject is accepted, why is it not simply the entire body, which perishes as one continuous identity when divided and is replaced by two other continuous bodies? You have already called it a substance, capable of dimensions and spatially situated in its own right; why must it inhere in something else? **Proposed reply:** The evident distinction between complete annihilation and genuine severance reveals a second abiding element. The Peripatetics call the form **inhering in** matter without calling it an accidental property **subsisting through** matter, since a substance cannot be degraded into an accident. **Al-Taftāzānī's challenge:** The proof must still show that the persisting thing is a **receptacle of the substantial form**, not merely the recipient of an **accidental continuity**. Calling the relation of form to matter a *qualifying attachment* (*ikhtiṣāṣ nāʿit*) cannot by itself establish it.

**Second difficulty:** Separating one body into two would require an underlying persisting subject only if separation were a **positive property**. But it is merely the **absence of continuity**. **Reply:** This is not sheer absence; it is the **absence of a continuity in a thing of which continuity is possible**. The process comprises the removal of one individual continuity and the occurrence of two new continuous identities. The Peripatetic requires something capable of either condition.

**Third difficulty:** If what admits separation needs a further matter, then **matter itself** admits separation and needs another matter, leading to an infinite regress. **Reply:** What requires matter is a thing continuous **in itself**, such that its individual substantial continuity perishes when separation occurs. Prime matter is not itself a continuous extension or a divided spatial aggregate. It receives continuity and plurality while remaining numerically the abiding potential recipient. Neither a first extended matter nor an actual manifold of material pieces is presupposed.

**Fourth difficulty:** If substantial continuity is a **part of body**, loss of that part destroys the body; but if the body **receives separation**, something bearing the name body must remain when separation occurs. How can body both perish and persist? One cannot settle this by distinguishing a substantial extension that perishes from an accidental measurement that changes. If the substantial form perishes, the whole body does not remain as such; if only the accidental extension changes, the supposed need for distinct **matter** has not been demonstrated. The wax changes its particular dimensions while remaining the same body, so the mere alternation of measurements proves no separate material recipient of corporeal form. **Peripatetic reply:** “Body admits separation” does **not** mean that body survives with **all its essential constituents** unchanged. It means that it contains a constituent that survives both before and after severance and is in the strict sense the recipient. Thus the difference between water's total annihilation and its division is preserved through matter, even while its prior **substantial continuity** is replaced by other individual continuities. **Author's concern:** It is hardly obvious that what survives is simply a bare part of the *water's essence*, rather than the water under a different individual configuration; the inference demands further argument.

**Fifth difficulty:** When one body's continuous identity becomes two bodies, do both inherit the **same single matter** or different matters? One numerically one matter in distinct spatial places under two corporeal forms is absurd. If the matters already existed separately before severance, the supposedly one body had **actual distinct parts** all along, and an infinity of divisible portions seems to require infinitely many matters and forms. If the matters did not exist before, separation annihilates the original matter as well as its form, defeating the entire proof of a **persisting recipient**. **Peripatetic reply:** Both matters existed previously **under the state of unity**, and now exist **under plurality**. Because matter in itself is pure capacity, it need not be an intrinsically unitary extended thing that gets destroyed or an intrinsically plural thing composed of actual parts. Unity and plurality are ascribed following the states of the informing continuity. This repeats the answer to the third difficulty in another guise.

A further question concerns **celestial bodies** which, on the philosophical account, cannot suffer physical rupture. The possibility of conceptual division does not itself require an actually existing physical recipient. How then can the proof from physical separation establish prime matter in **every** body, including a heavenly sphere? A later discussion of the consequences of matter must supply an independent reply.

**Editorial note:** The essential dispute is the distinction among **mathematical body** (measured quantity), **corporeal form** (a substantial determination enabling extension), **prime matter** (the potential recipient), and the **whole natural body**. Do not collapse inherence of form in matter into the inherence of an accident in a self-subsisting substance, nor suppose the difference is secured simply by terminology. The author explicitly challenges the proof's success while reconstructing the Peripatetic argument.

title: The Illuminationist alternative and the challenge to prime matter
en:
**Source:** digital I.307–309, canonical characters 748826–753113 (exclusive). **Status:** new close source-ordered working rendering, with unresolved electronic readings.

**“The Illuminationists hold...”** These philosophers privilege a broadly Platonic way of **unveiling and direct inspection** over the Peripatetic reliance on dialectical research and demonstration. They regard body as **one continuous entity in itself**, as sense seems to present it, but they deny that it is compounded either of indivisible atoms or of **matter and corporeal form**. Rather, the body is a **substantial magnitude** (*miqdār jawharī*) that persists through the changing accidental measurements assigned to it. A lump of wax keeps the same amount of bodily magnitude as its length increases and its breadth decreases with alterations in shape. What changes is its extension **along particular directions**, not its underlying substantial corporeal magnitude. Separation does not mean the annihilation of this latter magnitude; it means the loss of **contact between two portions**. Confusion arises because the word *ittiṣāl* is used for both the continuing magnitude and the separable unity between portions.

Bodies which share universal corporeality differ through **determinate magnitudes** corresponding to their particular bodies, not through absolute magnitude corresponding to corporeality in general. A body, insofar as it can receive changing dispositions and determinate species, may be **called matter** in an extended usage; and the alternating determinations **forms**. But this terminology does not imply two independently real constituent substances, one recipient and one inhering corporeal form.

The Illuminationists level several objections against the main Peripatetic argument.

**First:** If the “extension” or “continuity” in question means the **self-subsisting substance extended in spatial directions and capable of dimensions**, why not identify it with **body itself**? If it means the ordinary relation of being **joined** or **continuous**, this is an **accident**, not a substance; calling it an essential constituent of body or the first apprehended bodily substance is unwarranted. What persists in wax while its particular dimensions vary may be merely **extension in general**, maintained through successive particular magnitudes, much as “shape” is truly predicated in every stage even though the individual shapes vary. There need not be a single fixed additional thing over and above all those particular features. If the Peripatetic points instead to what is lost when one piece of wax is cut into two, that is the **accidental unity or conjunction of its supposed parts**. The **body** remains, while the former conjunction ceases. A separative continuity is dependent and needs a subject; it cannot be the second substantial constituent. Conversely, what has dimensions in itself and can subsist independently is **already body**, whatever name “substantial extended identity” is given to it.

**Second:** Extension is one **nature**; how could one example or subspecies be a substance while another is an accident? If the philosophers merely stipulate that some substances should be called extensions, their usage does not establish a different **substance within** a body in addition to body itself.

**Third:** Suppose corporeal extension and accidental extension are two distinct actualities in the same body. If one exceeds the other in magnitude, the excess must be **in a locus**; neither an accident nor a substantial form can be realised without its appropriate recipient. If they are equal in every direction, the argument from spatial identity against their plurality becomes powerful. The Peripatetic answers that their natures differ and their recipients differ: the accidental extension occurs in substantial form or body, while the substantial form has **prime matter** as its recipient. Their not being separately distinguished by the senses is no refutation. But that reply presupposes the very reality of two underlying natures whose demonstration is disputed.

Al-Rāzī raises a further **counter-demonstration**. Were prime matter real, it would either be spatially located (*mutaḥayyiz*) in itself or not. If not located at all, how could a corporeal form essentially bound to place and direction **inhere** in it? Nothing suggests that the immaterial intellect can be the physical receptacle of a body. If matter is spatially located, its location is either **independent** or **derivative**. If independently located, matter and corporeal form seem to share the distinctive property of independently spatial substances, becoming **similar things** which on the proposed principles cannot inhere in one another; why must the form depend on the matter rather than vice versa? If both were independent, there would be no inherence; if both dependent, matter would need further matter without end. If matter is located **derivatively**, by reason of corporeal form, it seems to be an accidental feature **inhering in corporeal form** rather than the other way around. If derivative spatial location sufficed to make something a recipient of body, why not equally claim that body is a property inhering in a colour?

**Reply:** The absence of independently spatial existence does not make matter an **accident in form**. Matter's condition for being located may be **the presence of corporeal form in it**, without making the matter a property of that form. Not everything whose spatial location requires another thing is an accident inhering in that other. Nor does a shared ability to have independent spatial location prove two substances identical in essence: spatiality may be a common consequence, not the **most specific essential attribute** establishing likeness. Even if two substances are alike in essence, likeness entails common **essential concomitants**, not necessarily all contingent and relational predicates. The argument as given therefore does not decisively refute matter.

**End of the third investigation:** This new working sequence reaches the heading **المبحث الرابع في تفاريع المذاهب**, the fourth investigation, which remains to be translated. The text establishes disagreement over whether body is one continuous substance, a hylomorphic composite, an aggregate of atoms, or a conjunction of subtler bodies. None of these reported positions should be mistaken for al-Taftāzānī's unqualified own doctrine without inspecting the individual replies.

title: Fourth investigation: consequences of the competing accounts of body
en:
**Source:** digital I.309–316, canonical characters 753113–771267 (exclusive). **Status:** new continuous close explanatory working translation, printed collation outstanding.

**“The fourth investigation: consequences of the doctrines.”** Several questions follow from the theologians' account that a body is composed of **indivisible substances**.

Do individual atoms admit **life** and attributes conditioned by life, including knowledge, power and will? Al-Ashʿarī and some early Muʿtazilites permit this; later Muʿtazilites deny it. The question turns on whether life requires a particular bodily **structure** (*binya*), discussed earlier. May an atom touch **the joint between two atoms**? Al-Ashʿarī denies it because that would divide the touching atom; Abū Hāshim and Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār permit it. Can a line of atoms be made **circular**? Al-Ashʿarī denies, al-Juwaynī permits; the prior geometrical arguments explain the dispute.

Does an atom have a **shape**? Al-Rāzī reports al-Ashʿarī's denial and a contrary Muʿtazilite majority. Al-Āmidī reports agreement that atoms do not properly possess shape, since a bounded figure would have an interior and boundary and thereby be divisible; the disagreement would be only which figure the atom **resembles**. Some say a sphere, because a polygon differs according to sides; others a triangle, the simplest polygon; others a square, which joins in a plane without gaps. Al-Rāzī suspects the intended resemblance is a **cube**, because six other atoms can join one atom on six sides. Arguments that every finite thing must be bounded by one boundary (sphere) or several (polygon) are answered by distinguishing not extending infinitely from **having a further enclosing extremity**. An indivisible atom can itself be the ultimate boundary where a composite ends.

Authorities also debate whether an atom has any **length, breadth, depth, volume or area**. If length or breadth in the literal quantitative sense belongs to it, that apparently entails division. The statement attributed to Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Ṣāliḥī that an atom is a body without length, width or depth should not be casually turned into the absurd claim that it possesses measurable dimensions. Al-Āmidī reports agreement that it has a share in **area**, but this is ambiguous. If the “share” is a spatial magnitude, why would the part not divide? If it means merely that adding atoms increases the occupied extent, the same indirect claim could be made about length and width. Ibn al-Rāwandī attributes some share in length to an atom. Abū ʿAlī and Abū Hāshim agree that it has none of length, since length follows the assembly of parts in a particular direction. They disagree about area: Abū ʿAlī regards it likewise as a product of juxtaposition, whereas Abū Hāshim takes **area** as a name for the atom's occupied space or bulk in virtue of which assembled atoms have increased volume.

Further disputes concern whether one atom has **directions**, whether it can be **seen**, whether it can be made as **heavy as a mountain**, how many atoms may contact it, whether God may create it **alone**, whether motion and rest can inhere in it alternately, and whether multiple accidents can simultaneously inhere in it. Al-Taftāzānī expressly declines to reproduce all the minute permutations from the longer disputational works, asking that his book not be faulted for omitting disputes with little useful purpose.

Proponents of minute **Democritean bodies**, divisible in imagination but not by physical separation, disagree about their shapes. Many make them **spherical** because spheres are simple, but then must admit a void between them. Others propose cubes, triangles or squares. Another scheme makes the primitive particles five kinds of regular solids: tetrahedra for fire, cubes for earth, octahedra for air, icosahedra for water and dodecahedra for the celestial substance. The *Shifāʾ* reports different shapes and, in some versions, the five regular solids. Both the strict atomists and the proponents of minute physically indivisible bodies generally take the basic constituents to be **alike in substance**, assigning differences among gross bodies to their accidents or to constituent **shapes**. Whether some resulting accidents must enter the very **essence of a species of body** remains a question.

### Five consequences of the Peripatetic view of matter and form

This distinction is intended to rule out the supposition that only certain **species** of body require matter. Yet it does not eliminate the possibility that dependence on matter arises from a **special accident**, such as physical susceptibility to cutting. The *Ishārāt* replies that the ability to be divided reveals a **pre-existing essential need** of corporeality for matter; it is an evidential sign, not the causal ground of the need. Al-Taftāzānī notes that the inference may still be denied. Another reply says every body intrinsically admits physical separation despite obstacles such as its spherical celestial nature, smallness or hardness. The suggestion that mere **imagined division** establishes a material subject is criticised because division in thought need not destroy continuity in external reality. To establish external matter, the imagined division must be shown to correspond to a **real external possibility of separate parts**, and that is precisely what is at issue.

**Second: prime matter cannot exist without some corporeal form.** Were it unformed it would either possess a position—being indicated as *here* or *there*—or not. If inherently spatial and capable of dimensions, it would already be **body**, not bare matter, given the rejection of an indivisible or line-like spatial substance. If not spatial, why should its later reception of form place it in **this particular region** rather than any other, when corporeal form relates indifferently to all regions? A specific elemental or species-form could be invoked, but then its selection, and that of its specific place, requires explanation. The movement of a portion of air that turns into water and then earth provides a possible natural account of determining position through earlier forms and subsequent downward motion. Still, matter might possess special conditions **other than forms and positions** which explain its eventual location, and this possibility is not excluded. Replies invoke either **separation or alteration**, each requiring a recipient, or distinguish the composite's continuing ability to receive forms from the relation of its portions to the whole. # MQ-C04-013 — Bodies: specific identities, persistence, place, and the necessity of accidents

**Arabic source:** *Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid*, electronic JK001157, source characters 771267–780567 (exclusive); printed-volume indicators I.317–320. **English status:** source-ordered explanatory first-pass translation. It is not yet a clause-verified diplomatic translation.

## The fifth investigation: the properties of bodies

Having discussed what a body is, we turn to its properties. Among them, according to the theologians, is that **bodies are alike in their real nature** (*mutamāthila*, united in *ḥaqīqa*), differing only through accidents. Upon this principle, they build a number of doctrines of Islam, including proof of the voluntary agent, and many matters of prophecy and resurrection. For the assignment of these determinate properties to each body requires a **specifying voluntary preference** (*murajjiḥ mukhtār*): a cause that acts by necessitation stands in the same relationship to the alternatives. Once the properties found in any body are admissible in every other—coldness in fire, burning in water—extraordinary occurrences conveyed in reports of miracles and of the Resurrection are shown to be possible.

For the theologians, the basis of this proposition is that the parts of body are none other than indivisible substances, and these substances are themselves alike: no diversity of intrinsic specific nature can be conceived in them. Whoever admits that the constituent atoms are alike but the resulting bodies differ in essential nature must make some accidents constituents of those differing natures. Some reason that bodies agree in occupying a region and receiving accidents, among their most characteristic properties; or that the genus body divides into celestial and elemental kinds, and the subject of a division must be common; or that bodies could be mistaken for one another were their accidents made the same. All these arguments are weak.

A distinguished philosopher has misunderstood what the theologians mean, taking their assertion of the sameness of bodies to say only that their **concept of corporeality** is common, even though the bodies themselves belong to different species beneath that concept. He relies on the fact that the definition of body, however formulated by a school, is one without a division within it: body is that which receives three dimensions, or that which possesses them, a definition extending to both natural and mathematical body. If several diverse things are collected under one definition, their division would have to be expressly introduced, he says. The misunderstanding arises from his finding it incredible that anyone would regard water and fire as one reality differing only through accidents, just as no one would deny the differentiae which constitute the various animal species. But the theologians are making the stronger claim. Nor does al-Naẓẓām's appeal to the differing special properties of bodies establish that the basic notion defined by corporeality is multiple: that argument can show difference of **species** rather than difference in the common definition.

### Do bodies persist?

Another property is that **bodies remain through two instants or more**. Necessity, it is said, tells us that our books, garments, houses, and animals are numerically the same things they formerly were: their accidental characteristics and configurations may alter, but their substances are not continuously replaced. This is not the claim that sensation itself directly witnesses persistence; otherwise an opponent could answer that like bodies are continually renewed, as is sometimes said of accidents. *Persistence* may also mean perpetual continuance or the impossibility of annihilation. It is in this latter sense that one can understand the assertion in *al-Tajrīd* that necessity certifies the permanence of bodies, because the worst that happens to them is dispersal or division, neither of which annihilates their underlying reality.

But a claim of necessity here, in the stronger sense, is highly unsound. The possible annihilation of bodies has itself been acknowledged in the discussion of resurrection. One argues for the possibility of annihilation either from their **origination**, since a preceding nonexistence and a subsequent nonexistence have no intrinsic distinction, or from their **possibility**, meaning that existence and nonexistence are both admissible when the essence is taken in itself. A reply points out that neither argument excludes **impossibility owing to another** (*imtināʿ bi-l-ghayr*): a thing could be capable of nonexistence in itself, yet prevented by a cause from undergoing an earlier or later nonexistence. Origination, then, need not exclude endless continuance—the rational soul, on Aristotle's account, provides a case—and possibility by essence does not exclude either eternity without beginning or eternity without end, as the philosophers maintain of things temporally eternal but not necessary in themselves. General scriptural expressions such as “Every thing is perishing except His Face” and “Everyone upon it will perish” are also adduced. Even if the dissolution of composites is explained by the loss of their structure and specific forms, a simple body, or its underlying atoms or matter-and-form constituents, can perish in the stronger sense only through nonexistence.

A line of argument against an accident's persistence had asserted that if an accident remained, it could not subsequently cease. Since that argument would extend to bodies unless a distinction were made, **al-Naẓẓām** accepted that bodies do not survive two instants, but continually recur as newly created similars; the **Karrāmiyya**, by contrast, took persistence to be necessary and therefore accepted the impossibility of their annihilation. Each side affirms or rejects one member of the disputed implication through its account of the other. The implication's proof has already been refuted in the earlier investigation on whether accidents persist. There are also answers even if that implication were assumed: a body may cease when God no longer creates in it the accidents on which its continuance depends, such as the states of being located (*akwān*), according to the judge and Imām al-Ḥaramayn; or when God does not create an accident of **persistence**, as al-Kaʿbī proposes; or when God creates an accident of **annihilation**, whether a separate annihilator for each substance, as Abū ʿAlī maintains, or a single annihilation sufficient for all bodies, according to others.

The suggestion that al-Naẓẓām denies persistence simply because for him body is a bundle of accidents is incorrect. His doctrine is not that body is an accident, but that things others treat as accidents, such as colour, taste and odour, are bodies subsisting in themselves. Philosophers do not dispute that composites perish through loss of specific form and arrangement. The dispute concerns their **total** annihilation, including both prime matter and corporeal form; their denial follows their affirmation of these as beginningless, from which they infer that they cannot cease. Their arguments will be considered below.

### Figure and natural region

Every body must possess a **shape** because bodies are finite, and figure means nothing other than the disposition in which a body's extremity bounds it. That a body occupies a region (*ḥayyiz*), understood as the extension which it fills, is evident. Such evident propositions appear in scholarly inquiries where clarification, a further derivation, a dispute, or correction of an error is required. According to our school, the assignments of particular shapes and regions derive from the **voluntary agent**. The philosophers hold instead that each body possesses a **natural figure** and **natural region**: when free of every external constraint and violent cause, it occupies a determinate region with a determinate shape. The phrase *natural* designates precisely what belongs to it under this supposition, and therefore does not mean only an indeterminate shape or some unspecified region.

The natural region is not necessarily *place* in the narrow sense of the inner surface of the surrounding body, which would fail for a body with no surrounding place, such as the outermost sphere; neither is it simply a void occupied by the body. Ibn Sīnā says that every body has a natural region, which, **if it has a place**, will be that place; elsewhere he adds that no body is without a region, whether it is a place or an ordered positional arrangement. One might object that the particular natural region cannot follow from generic corporeality or its necessary properties, but must be determined by something special; the answer invokes the earlier account of **specific substantial forms**.

The philosophers agree that a body has **only one natural region**. The one nature, they say, has one necessary effect. Were two natural regions assigned to a body, then, in the absence of a violent cause, either it would occupy both, which is impossible, or it would occupy one and the other would not be natural. Likewise, once an externally displaced body were freed, it would either move toward both, an impossibility; move toward one, making the other a naturally rejected region; or move toward neither, in which case neither functions as its natural destination. It may be suggested that contingent specifying circumstances choose between the two. But the hypothesis removes all **extrinsic** conditions. Nonetheless a further objection persists: perhaps neither is obtained, because each candidate prevents the other and no one is preferred without a specifier; the body simply stays where it is. The author of *al-Mawāqif* treats this theory of natural region as a consequence of the doctrine of prime matter, since advocates of indivisible atoms maintain that bodies have essentially the same nature and differ only in accidents.

### Can a body be devoid of accidents?

The apparent positions of **prohibition** and **permission** here are not precisely contradictories. According to the stronger prohibitive doctrine associated with many theologians, a body capable of a genus of accidents must at every relevant time have **one of the alternatives** belonging to that genus. Al-Rāzī's *Nihāyat al-ʿUqūl* states this in terms of one of the two contraries under every relevant class. Imām al-Ḥaramayn describes the doctrine as follows: a substance is never free of the genus of accidents and its contraries—where there is one contrary it must have one or the other, and where a genus has no contrary it must bear an instance of the genus. No one disagrees that a body cannot be stripped of every relevant accident after possessing them, on this view. The permissive doctrine says that a body may lack **all accidents**, either from eternity, as held by those who make substances beginningless but their attributes originated, or at some later time, as maintained by the Ṣāliḥiyya among the Muʿtazila.

Thus one view asserts a **universal affirmative**—every body must bear a member from every relevant class—whereas the opposite asserts the possibility of a **universal negative**, that it bears none. The more plausible intermediate assertion is the **particular affirmative**, that every body must have *some accident*. Those giving a narrower rule differ: the Baghdadi Muʿtazilites require some **colour**, while the Basrans require some form of **being-located** (*kawn*), such as motion or rest and combination or separation.

The prohibitive argument that a body must be temporally present and numerically determinate can establish at most that some motion/rest or combination/separation must accompany it, not that it possess an accident of every genus. This does answer anyone who permits complete absence of accidents, and it challenges the Baghdadi position that all other genera may be absent. Similarly, whatever exists must be **individuated**, and if bodies are composed of essentially alike atoms, their differentiation must come from accidents. But **some** individuating accident suffices; the argument does not make an accident from every genus indispensable. This proof might, unlike the first, cover every time, including an allegedly timeless beginning, because individuation does not depend on motion or on the simultaneous presence of another body. One could try to universalize by analogy: a substance is qualified either by essence or by its receptivity, and supposedly these stand equally to all accident genera at all times. Both propositions can be denied.

Proponents of possible absence offer several considerations. First, if God could not create a body without creating an accident in it, His choice would supposedly be constrained. **Reply:** not being able to instantiate a contradiction—here a body together with the absence of something necessarily entailed by its existence—does not remove choice or constitute impotence. Second, if a body cannot be free of combination and separation, God could not create a **first body** before all others, an unacceptable result; these relational accidents plainly require a second body. Third, if it could not lack every colour, how could **air**, apparently colourless, exist? To reply that colour is simply imperceptible raises the problem that where the sense is sound and ordinary conditions obtain, a perceptible quality's persistent nonappearance is evidence of absence. Resorting indiscriminately to unseen impediments would license the belief that giant mountains and tremendous sounds are present before us but somehow unperceived. A different answer, however, says **transparency** (*shafāfiyya*) is the contrary of colour rather than its simple absence.

*Editorial note:* This chapter continually separates (a) the common concept of body, (b) one and the same **specific** corporeal reality, (c) numerically distinct individual bodies, and (d) the accidental principles of individuation. Those propositions must not be fused in translation.
